articles.title: Iran, US presidents sign deal to extend ceasefire, reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Both sides confirm signing a memorandum of understanding that extends their ceasefire by 60 days.
articles.body:
The United States and Iran have electronically signed a memorandum of understanding to extend their ceasefire and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said late on Wednesday that the agreement had gone into effect.

“The text of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding was finalised with the signatures of the presidents,” Baghaei told the news agency IRNA. “Now it is time to test the implementation of the agreement.”

Trump told reporters that he had signed the memorandum with Iran at the Palace of Versailles, near the French capital, Paris.

“It’s signed,” Trump said as he left Versailles. “I signed it in Versailles,” he added. “Just signed it.”

The White House later confirmed that Trump ⁠had signed ⁠the breakthrough agreement.

Since February 28, the US and Israel have been jointly engaged in a war against Iran, though a temporary ceasefire suspended much of the most intense fighting on April 8. This agreement extends the ceasefire for 60 days, with Iran gradually reopening the strait and the US lifting its blockade of Iranian ports.

The agreement paves the way for further negotiations over Iran’s nuclear programme. In return, the US will move to waive some wide-ranging sanctions against Iran.

Given that both sides signed the agreement electronically, Baghaei noted that there would not be a signing ceremony on Friday in Geneva, Switzerland, as had previously been expected.

Negotiating teams, however, still plan to be in the Swiss city. A decision on a possible in-person meeting between them is expected in the coming hours, though for now such plans are paused, according to Baghaei.

Video footage of the moment the US president physically signed the interim deal at the Versailles Palace showed him pausing before putting pen to paper.

“This was not easy,” Trump told his audience, holding out his hands. “I can tell you that,” he added as he signed the first page.

Iran will monitor US compliance without ‘leniency’

Baghaei addressed Iranian media following the signing, stating that Iran will monitor the US’s compliance “without any leniency” and will not “fulfil” its commitments if Washington “evades its obligations”.

He also said that Iran’s nuclear programme and the lifting of US sanctions would be discussed during the 60-day period, but that Tehran’s missile programme would be off the table.

“Iran’s missiles are only for firing, not for negotiation. Iran’s defence capabilities will not be discussed in any process with any party,” he said.

Baghaei additionally said Iran would not ship its stockpile of highly enriched uranium abroad, and that dilution of the material was “introduced as an option to close the door on other possibilities”.

Regarding Israel’s war on Lebanon, Baghaei said Iran has shown it “does not abandon its friends” and that it was the US’s responsibility to compel Israel to respect commitments to Iran.

On the Strait of Hormuz, Baghaei said Iran would finalise a new regime to manage the waterway along with Oman, and would “charge fees for services” there.

Al Jazeera’s correspondent Mike Hanna warned that the memorandum is likely to face domestic backlash in the US, where Trump has been under right-wing pressure to take a hard line against Iran.

“There’s a great deal of dissatisfaction with the memorandum of understanding, as it has been outlined to the public at this particular point, even among some Republicans who have expressed the concern that Iran is being treated leniently,” Hanna said.

He also emphasised the administration’s position that the memorandum is not a full-fledged deal, but a prelude to more negotiations.

“The administration is fighting hard to persuade the American public and American politicians that this is not a defeat for the United States,” Hanna said.

Trump has repeatedly said his goal in launching the war was to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

Since the memorandum was revealed, he has highlighted the document’s assurances that Iran will not seek a nuclear weapon, though Tehran has long denied any intention of doing so.

But according to a US account, the memo goes beyond the question of nuclear weapons. It sets up a 60-day timeline for a final deal to be struck, and it indicates that the US will rally “regional partners” to create a $300bn fund for Iran’s reconstruction.

The US would also work towards easing some sanctions against Iran, and the country would issue waivers for the export of Iranian fuel.

Iran has touted the agreement as a victory. On Wednesday, chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf told Fars, an Iranian state news agency, that the US had failed to achieve its goals with Iran, and pointed to the memo as proof.

“The agreement is a record of US failure,” Ghalibaf said. “People will see it and judge.”

Iran’s position on Hormuz, meanwhile, is likely to put pressure on the Trump administration, which had pledged that the strait, a key waterway for trade, would be “permanently toll-free”.

Since the start of the war, Iran has effectively blocked the waterway, sending global prices for fuel, fertiliser and other goods soaring.

The US responded with its own blockade of Iranian ports, though that effort is slated to end under the memorandum.

Both sides, however, have emphasised that the memorandum of understanding is not a final settlement.

“It will only become a deal, as such, at the end of the 60-day negotiation period. At least, that’s the intention,” Hanna reported.

articles.title: Gwynedd house with no roof up for auction for £17k
articles.summary: It's been home to north Wales' strongest man Dewi Arfon near Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon.
articles.body:
With property prices soaring in recent years, the idea of buying your own home for £17,000 might seem like a dream come true.

But there's a catch - it doesn't have a roof.

The "ruined shell" of 400-year-old Ty Du near Llanberis, Gwynedd, lies in the wooded foothills of Wales' highest mountain, Yr Wyddfa, also know as Snowdon .

It dates from the 13th Century, and once belonged to the Goodman family of Ruthin. In 1650 Godfrey Goodman - the Bishop of Gloucester - was banished there by Oliver Cromwell for his religious beliefs.

Over the years, it has also been home to north Wales' strongest man, and in the 19th Century, a poet called Dewi Arfon, according to Auction House.

The house is thought to have begun as a platform house, being rebuilt in the 17th Century as a storied house.

Auction House said it was listed in the Inventory of the Royal Commission as an important domestic building in the parish.

The auctioneers said the ruined property has intact walls to eaves level, as well as two ruined cottages, a smithy and old shop.

The owners on Anglesey, they added, have preserved the A-frame roof and other timbers.

At the back of the house there is an old pack horse trail that once connected Llanberis to Caernarfon.

articles.title: Coast Guard finds debris field off Nantucket after Boston-bound medevac plane vanishes with 6 on board
articles.summary: A Gulfstream G100 with 6 people on board vanished en route to Boston from Bermuda on Saturday as search crews deploy off Nantucket to conduct a search. Offic...
articles.body:
U.S. Coast Guard confirms debris field off Nantucket coast linked to missing medevac flight with six people on board.

Search efforts ongoing for potential survivors, Coast Guard cutter William Sparling to continue search throughout the night.

Gulfstream G100 twin-engine jet disappeared en route from Bermuda to Boston, FAA reported losing contact with the aircraft early Saturday.

U.S. Coast Guard search crews located a debris field off the Nantucket coast that has been confirmed to be associated with a medevac flight with six people on board that disappeared Saturday morning while en route to Boston from Bermuda.

Crews are continuing to search for potential survivors, and the Coast Guard cutter William Sparling will continue search efforts throughout the night. The Coast Guard said it would hold a news conference Sunday morning.

Authorities are searching for the Gulfstream G100, a twin-engine, midsize jet, off Nantucket. Both air and surface crews have been deployed to the area, according to the Coast Guard Northeast District.

The Federal Aviation Administration ( Faa ) reported losing contact with the aircraft early Saturday, the Coast Guard said.

Earlier Saturday, the FAA issued a statement that said it is "coordinating with the Rescue Coordination Center and the U.S. Coast Guard to locate the aircraft."

According to data from FlightAware, the plane took off from Bermuda L. F. Wade International Airport at 11:41 p.m. ET.

The FAA told Fox News Digital it issued a Search and Rescue Alert Notice at about 1:20 a.m. ET.

The Massachusetts Port Authority (Massport), which operates the state's three major airports, confirmed that the aircraft did not arrive at Boston Logan International Airport as scheduled.

"Our thoughts are with those on board and their loved ones as the search continues," the agency said.

The Canadian -registered aircraft is owned by Latitude Air Ambulance, the company confirmed to Fox News Digital, adding that it was a medevac flight.

Two Canadian pilots, two medical workers, one patient and a patient's companion were on board.

Latitude Air Ambulance is a medical transport company that brings patients home from around the world when they require specialized care.

Latitude Air Ambulance said the flight was supposed to take about two hours.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) told Fox News Digital that it is currently gathering information and declined to provide an update on the situation.

"My thoughts are with the six people aboard the missing air ambulance traveling from Bermuda to Boston, and their families," Bermuda's Premier David Burt said in a statement. "Government has contacted the family and US search and rescue authorities. We are praying that everyone will be found safe."

The plane plummeted from 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet in just three minutes at around 1 a.m., according to data from FlightAware.

Skyport, the company that manages the airport in Bermuda, confirmed that a "Canadian-registered air ambulance departed L. F. Wade International Airport for Boston at approximately 12:41 am on Saturday, October 3, 2026, with six souls on board, including four crew members and two passengers."

"The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration has advised that air traffic controllers lost contact with the aircraft off the coast of Nantucket Island, Massachusetts, and a search is currently underway. Skyport has no further information to provide at this time," the company added.

"This aircraft was dealt a dire one-two punch: a critical safety in-flight problem, followed almost immediately by a perilous weather event and an 11,000-foot plunge," former U.S. Department of Transportation Inspector General Mary Schiavo said in analysis shared with Fox News Digital.

As of Saturday afternoon, the Coast Guard has deployed a HC-130 Hercules crew from Coast Guard Air Station Elizabeth City, New Jersey; a MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew from Coast Guard Air Station Cape Cod; a 47-foot motor lifeboat crew from Coast Guard Station Brant Point, Massachusetts; and Coast Guard Cutter William Sparling, a Boston-based Fast Response Cutter.

articles.title: CG village council resolution bars land for Christian burials, prayer meets
articles.summary: Punpalli gram sabha in Sukma, Chhattisgarh bars Christian burials, churches and prayer meets on village land; officials to review legality under PESA.
articles.body: Raipur: A special village council or gram sabha, convened at Punpalli village of Chhattisgarh’s Sukma district, passed a resolution to forbid any land it holds from being made available to Christians or converts from building churches, holding prayer meetings, burials or ‘healing’ gatherings.The council also resolved to put up a public notice barring pastors and Christian preachers from entering the village for ‘conversion’ or religious activity.The resolution, passed as decision number 6 of the special Gram Sabha, cites Article 244(1) of the Constitution, the fifth schedule, the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996, and Chhattisgarh’s PESA framework to justify the move, confirmed Madkam Bhima, a Janpad member.The notice, already erected at the entrance to the village, states not ‘an inch’ of Gram Sabha land would be given for burials of Christians or converts, churches, prayer meetings or faith healing sessions. It adds that pastors, priests and Christian preachers would not be allowed to enter Punpalli for conversion, prayer meetings or related religious activity.Bhima said the gram sabha adopted the resolution in keeping with the village’s traditional way of life, social unity and community interests, adding that any dispute should be dealt with through legal and constitutional processes.The development is especially significant as Punpalli lies in a Scheduled Area, where PESA vests gram sabhas substantial powers to safeguard tribal traditions, customs, cultural identity, community resources and customary methods of dispute resolution. The central PESA Act explicitly recognises those powers.However, the legislation, while safeguarding tribal customs and identities, does not expressly state that a gram sabha can exclude people from community land solely on the basis of their faith, thereby making the scope and legal enforceability of the Punpalli resolution a contentious subject.The issue acquires particular sensitivity for Bastar, where disputes over conversion, burial rights and the religious identity of tribal communities have repeatedly triggered confrontations.In January 2025, the Supreme Court had to intervene in a Chhattisgarh burial dispute, after a Christian tribal family from Bastar claimed to have been prevented from burying a deceased family member in the village. The case brought to the fore the underlying tension and conflict between local customary claims, burial practices and constitutional rights.The Punpalli council said its decision was aimed at protecting the village’s cultural identity, traditional practices and social heritage. The resolution was displayed prominently on a notice board so that not just locals but also visitors are aware of it.Among those present at the gram sabha were sarpanch Sonmati Madvi, council president Barse Soma, deputy sarpanch Muchaki Nanda, village Patel (headman) Barse Pandu and other traditional and elected representatives.Officials said the administration would examine the resolution and the notice put up in Punpalli to determine whether the decisions are in keeping with the powers vested in the council under PESA and other applicable laws.However, they did acknowledge that gram sabhas in Scheduled Areas have an important role in protecting customary practices, traditions and community resources.“The contents of the resolution and the circumstances in which it was passed will be looked into. articles.title: Delhi hit-and-run: Couple in  70s flung into air after SUV hits them, driver held after fleeing spot
articles.summary: Elderly Kirti Nagar couple injured after SUV hit from behind; driver fled but later arrested. Police registered FIR, impounded vehicle, reviewing CCTV and phone use.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A 79-year-old man and his 71-year-old wife were injured after an SUV allegedly hit them from behind near Arya Samaj Mandir in west Delhi’s Kirti Nagar Friday. CCTV footage showed that the driver got out of the car, checked on the injured couple and fled. She was arrested later.The injured couple were identified as Dayanand and Kusum Tagra, residents of Kirti Nagar. They have been hospitalised and are recovering, police said. Their children are based in US. The accused was identified as 49-year-old Navleen Kaur, a homemaker and a resident of Kirti Nagar. Her husband is a businessman, said police.CCTV footage showed the elderly couple walking along the road when the grey SUV hit them from behind with considerable force. The impact threw Dayanand onto the bonnet and he landed on his head. Kusum, who was using crutches, fell to the side.Passersby rushed to help the couple. Dayanand, who had lost consciousness, can be seen lying in the middle of the road and bleeding from his head. The footage also showed the driver getting out of the vehicle after the collision. She appeared to check on the injured couple and was seen moving around the spot before allegedly getting back into the car and driving away.Police said an FIR was registered at Kirti Nagar police station under sections 281 (rash driving or riding on a public way) and 125(a) (penalty for rash driving) of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. Police have impounded the vehicle.Kaur allegedly told police that she was driving home when she suddenly “blacked out”. Investigators are probing whether she was using her mobile phone at the time of the accident.Police are examining the CCTV footage and other evidence to reconstruct the sequence of events and establish whether any other factor contributed to the crash.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: When the menu is the message
articles.summary: Twenty years ago, a pucca Lucknawi gentleman was talking about life in the old days.
articles.body: Twenty years ago, a pucca Lucknawi gentleman was talking about life in the old days. His family was Muslim, but they had many Hindu friends who would come for family celebrations. Since many of them would not eat otherwise, brahmins would be hired to cook and serve them in a separate shamiana.In other words, you could be close friends and yet be respectful of cultural distances. It was a gracious expression of tolerance and liberality, but it made me uncomfortable: is it necessarily okay to indulge the abhorrent prejudices of your guests? If brahmins refuse food served by lower castes, should they stay home?I was reminded of that slightly troubling discussion by the recent controversy about whether it was appropriate to serve our Brics visitors a (pretty wonderful) fully vegetarian meal. As a regular menu-planner, I was not troubled by the fact that it was not representative of what most Indians eat. Menus must have an internal balance — the paneer lababdar, all cream and cashews might go better with a lighter dal (like the thakkali bele saaru they served with it) than a hearty mah di dal. And in any case, we have so much to showcase, even sticking to vegetarian dishes, that we could have fed them for a month without running out of interesting offerings.What bothered me is what our visitors made of it. When I plan a meal, I think hard about what my guests will enjoy. I might want to surprise them a little, intrigue them a bit, even throw in a soupçon of culinary education, but my main goal is that they go home happy and well-fed. I don’t know this for a fact, but I strongly suspect that for most invitees, vegetarian food is something that one eats as penance or when on a strict diet. This is perhaps why the Chinese president stayed away. Maybe some of the others sneaked out for a secret midnight snack after the gala dinner!This is what made me think of that Lucknow conversation. Whereas my acquaintance was willing to accommodate his guests’ preferences, the decision in Delhi was to give primacy to “ours”. Even if the goal was to persuade our guests that our vegetarian food was as subtle and wonderful as anything the non-vegetarian world has to offer — which I fully accept — there could still have been some choice; the meal could have started, as it often does in fancy restaurants, with a short speech about the special vegetarian dishes that were being served. Or did someone actually intend to hint at “our” disapproval of our guests’ food habits? Atithi devo bhava, but only if they eat the right foods.Food is now so political everywhere in India, that it is hard to rule this out. Just the other day, a certain Bageshwar baba created a small crisis in West Bengal politics by advising Bengalis to go vegetarian for Durga Puja. Even the CM decided that this was too much, and had himself filmed eating an enormous piece of fish. A few days later, a child in a Mumbai school had to pay a fine for bringing green methi (!!!) for lunch, which apparently “hurt the sentiments” of the Jain kids.I can only speculate about what happened in Delhi, but I can imagine that even without any directive from up top, the person choosing the menu would be in a bit of a quandary. She/he might want a menu that everyone enjoys, but would the inclusion of say, a kosha mangsho, be seen as insufficiently respectful of the preferences of our strictly vegetarian top leadership? Indeed, if there was something like that on the menu, optional of course, would the committed vegetarians on the guest list feel compelled to protest that this is not their Indian tradition? And on the other hand, if they try to be understanding and choose not to protest, would they be considered insufficiently committed to the cause of building a Hindu nation? Would there be a scandal in the right-wing press? Would heads roll?Food may be particularly salient in India, perhaps thanks to the strong connection between ritual purity and diet in Hindu religious practice, but the challenge of navigating identity markers is everywhere now. Not just whether a Hindu should eat meat (the first-order identity marker), but also whether a Hindu should serve meat (second-order marker), and even whether a Hindu should be friends with someone who serves meat to others (a third-order marker). Every one of these is now a signal that someone else might be reading, interpreting and potentially reacting to, and therefore every one of us needs to go through an intellectual double or triple take every time we decide on little things that used to be automatic. As it is for a Muslim woman who does or doesn’t cover her head, or has to decide whether to associate with others who do or don’t. Or for a BJP supporter who just wants India to play Test cricket again with Pakistan, so that we can show them how much better we are. Is he guilty of ignoring the pain of all those who suffered from terrorism, or just a cricket lover who wants an exemption for his passion? And would it be okay for another BJP supporter to speak out in his defence?There is a game-theoretic argument that might help us understand how we got to these paralysing ambiguities. Imagine a world where people have diverse personal opinions that they value, but also some preference for conformity. In a world where everyone speaks their mind, there is no one public opinion to go against — if you try to be like A, you will be less like B or C — so you might as well indulge your individuality. Diversity breeds diversity.Now think of the reverse. Assume for a moment that for whatever reason, everyone else opts to keep their opinions private and pays lip service to a single collective view. Then taking a different position becomes more costly, since now you would be going against what appears to be everyone’s opinion. Maybe you will also opt to stay silent. Conformity feeds on itself.The same argument would hold if the community were polarised between, say, a left orthodoxy and a right orthodoxy. Those who are uncomfortable with both, might either stay silent or shade their public position towards whichever they are less uncomfortable with.While both conformity and diversity are potential options for this imaginary community, the presence of enforcers, people who will attack you at the slightest show of difference, tends to push us towards the former. Moreover, if you happen to be the lone dissenting view, you must worry that the enforcers will all come for you, which must be frightening. This is exactly the effect that the armies of AI-aided right-wing trolls in India aim for (as does President Trump), but there are also enforcers on the left — including those who will come after you for using the wrong pronoun or not being pure enough in your anti-capitalist views.Diversity feels worryingly fragile these days, in the sense that a small number of powerful and ruthless voices can drown the rest. One can be punished not only for deviating, but also for tolerating other suspected deviants. This is what has happened to the Republican Party in the US, where everyone either toes the full Trump line or endures the career-ending force of his fury. And even in India, while I hear a lot of grumbling (especially now), most people won’t publicly protest.Part of the problem is social media. It is easy to enforce compliance if you are quick on the keyboard, ruthless, and comfortable claiming the moral high ground (like Trump). On the other hand, I don’t want to suggest that there was once a now-lost paradise of unbridled liberality. For every Lucknawi who happily reached across religions, there were probably several who openly disdained the other. The much disparaged “woke” discourse was first and foremost an attempt to regulate the expression of naked prejudice — it is easy to forget just how bad things used to be, and still are in large chunks of the right. But it is hard not to see that it has turned into an arms race of virtue-signaling that divides the left at a time when it needs to unite, and distracts from all the daunting issues that need to be tackled.That said, calls for more honesty and openness can be treacherous, fronting some desire to be openly sexist, casteist, or racist when it suits us. But it is still worthwhile to try to be more tolerant of those with whom we mostly agree. If they have spent their life doing and saying the right things, let’s not jump to condemn them at the first sign of deviance. Let’s try to think of the best reason they might have gone that way. And allow for the possibility that it was an honest mistake. Or even that the misunderstanding might be ours.Recipe for Black Pepper Chicken/TofuI often design menus where a small last-minute tweak turns a dish vegetarian, so that I can serve both sets of clients with little effort. This pair is mostly for President Xi, if he has vegetarian guests.Make a marinade with 4 tbs hoisin sauce, 2 tbs light soy, 2 tbs dark soy, 4 tbs chinese cooking wine, 1tbs sesame oil, 2 tsp grated ginger, and 2 tbs cornstarch, whisking till the starch is dissolved (use vegan substitutes for soy if preferred). Divide in half and marinate separately 250 gms boneless chicken thigh and 250 gms of firm tofu, both cut into bite-sized morsels, for one hour in the fridge. Heat a medium-sized pan at high heat, and when the oil is visibly hot, add the chicken, stir-fry for a minute, and then reduce heat to medium and cook for 2 minutes (check that the meat is fully cooked through). Put the chicken on a plate and rinse the pan very carefully (or use a different pan) and repeat with the tofu (it should crisp up a bit).Make a sauce with 1/2 cup vegetable stock, 1 tbs light soy, 1.5 tbs dark soy, 1 tsp sugar, 2 tsp sesame oil and 1 tbs cornstarch. Heat 2 tbs peanut oil in a wok to medium-high, and fry together ½ cup sliced onion, 1 sliced capsicum, and ½ cup sliced celery for 1 minute. Add 2 tsp minced garlic and 1 tbs coarsely crushed black pepper. Fry for 1 minute more and take off heat. Take out half the vegetables, and then add the chicken and half the sauce. Cook till the sauce thickens (1-2 minutes). Pour into a serving bowl and cover. Rinse and dry the wok (or use another one), add the vegetables and heat at medium-high and then add tofu and sauce. Cook till the sauce thickens (1-2 minutes).Abhijit Banerjee is recipient of the 2019 Nobel Prize in economicsDisclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Voto de presos no DF: 383 detentos e menores votam nas Eleições 2026 | G1
articles.standfirst: Ao todo, 171 presos provisórios e 212 adolescentes em internação socioeducativa poderão votar no Distrito Federal. Direito é garantido àqueles que não têm condenação definitiva.
articles.summary: Voto de presos no DF é garantido a 383 detentos provisórios e adolescentes sem condenação definitiva, com urnas instaladas em unidades como a Papuda e a Colmeia.
articles.body:
Complexo Penitenciário da Papuda, no DF — Foto: TV Globo/Reprodução

Neste domingo (4), durante o primeiro turno das Eleições 2026, 171 presos provisórios e 212 adolescentes internados para cumprir medida socioeducativa devem exercer o direito ao voto no Distrito Federal.

A participação desses eleitores exige uma logística específica, que envolve a Justiça Eleitoral e a Justiça Comum – por exemplo, as Varas de Execuções Penais e de Execução de Medidas Socioeducativas do DF.

As urnas serão instaladas nas unidades que recebem presos provisórios no DF. São elas:

o Centro de Detenção Provisória (CDP), na Papuda;

o Centro de Progressão Penitenciária (CPP), no Setor de Indústria e Abastecimento (SIA);

a Penitenciária Feminina do DF (Colmeia), no Gama.

Haverá, também, seções eleitorais nas unidades de internação dos jovens em medida socioeducativa. O horário de votação nesses espaços é o mesmo válido para qualquer eleitor: das 8h às 17h .

A Constituição Federal prevê a suspensão dos direitos políticos em seu art. 15, inciso III – mas a regra só vale para quem tem condenação judicial definitiva (trânsito em julgado), e enquanto durar a condenação.

➡️ Ou seja: quem está cumprindo prisão temporária ou preventiva, mas ainda aguarda julgamento, tem seus direitos políticos preservados, incluindo o direito de votar .

Também têm direito a voto todos os adolescentes que cumprem medidas socioeducativas em centros de internação – e claro, que têm 16 anos completos ou mais.

Isso, porque no Brasil as medidas socioeducativas não suspendem os direitos políticos dos infratores.

A logística para a votação do primeiro turno nas unidades envolve organização de escoltas, instalação de equipamentos e articulação com equipes da Justiça Eleitoral. Por isso, algumas atividades de rotina terão as datas ajustadas.

No sistema prisional, os atendimentos de advogados no Centro de Detenção Provisória (CDP) serão suspensos no domingo (4), à exceção dos casos emergenciais.

A saída quinzenal do Centro de Progressão Penitenciária (CPP) e da Penitenciária Feminina do Distrito Federal (PFDF) foi antecipada para esta sexta (2), com retorno no sábado (3).

Nas demais unidades, os atendimentos de advogados serão mantidas regularmente.

No sistema socioeducativo, haverá suspensão de visita de familiares, atendimento de advogados, saídas especiais, saídas-teste, atividades religiosas e atividades educativas no domingo (4), exceto em situações de urgência.

articles.title: Paraná tem alerta vermelho de tempestade em 143 cidades neste domingo  | G1
articles.standfirst: Aviso de grande perigo prevê chuva acima de 100 milímetros por dia e possibilidade de granizo. Frente fria aumenta risco de temporais em diferentes regiões do estado.
articles.summary: Aviso de grande perigo prevê chuva acima de 100 milímetros por dia e possibilidade de granizo. Frente fria aumenta risco de temporais em diferentes regiões do estado.
articles.body:
O Paraná tem 142 cidades sob alerta vermelho de tempestade neste domingo (4), dia do primeiro turno das eleições de 2026. O aviso, de "grande perigo", é do Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet) e vale durante todo o dia.

Segundo o instituto, nas áreas abrangidas pelo alerta, a chuva pode passar de 60 milímetros por hora ou de 100 milímetros ao longo do dia. Também são previstas rajadas de vento acima de 100 km/h e queda de granizo.

O Inmet alerta para grande risco de danos em construções, interrupção no fornecimento de energia elétrica, queda de árvores, alagamentos, prejuízos em plantações e transtornos no transporte rodoviário.

Além das 142 cidades sob alerta vermelho, outras áreas do Paraná estão sob avisos laranja, de perigo, e amarelo, de perigo potencial, para tempestades.

chuva paraná estrada bela vista do paraíso tempestade nuvem céu — Foto: Bruna Melo/g1 Paraná

A previsão é de mudança nas condições do tempo neste domingo com o avanço de uma frente fria pelo Paraná.

Segundo a Climatempo, há condições para chuva forte e temporais em praticamente todo o estado, principalmente nas regiões Norte, Noroeste, Oeste, Sudoeste, Centro e em áreas do Sul. A previsão inclui raios, chuva intensa e fortes rajadas de vento. A Climatempo também aponta risco de temporais no Paraná durante o domingo com o avanço da frente fria.

As temperaturas também devem cair nas regiões com maior nebulosidade e chuva. Em Curitiba, a previsão é de mínima de 14°C e máxima de 21°C, com 95% de chance de chuva neste domingo.

Domingo, 4 de outubro — Foto: Reprodução/Simepar

No domingo, a instabilidade se intensifica e a chuva se espalha por praticamente todo o Paraná. A previsão da Climatempo aponta que a atuação de sistemas de baixa pressão associada ao avanço da frente fria favorece períodos de chuva e pancadas, com possibilidade de chuva forte, risco de ventanias, granizo e trovoadas, além de acumulados elevados, principalmente no oeste, norte e centro do Estado.

Os modelos do Simepar preveem que as tempestades devem se concentrar entre a madrugada e o início da manhã.

"Ao longo da tarde e noite alguns eventos de chuva ainda ocorrem, mas de forma mais pontual. Na segunda e terça-feira, o ambiente permanece bastante instável, devido à intensificação de um sistema de baixa pressão nos países vizinhos".

tempestade temporal chuva nuvem nuvens paraná pr céu — Foto: Paulo Silveira Padilha

Durante rajadas de vento, o Inmet orienta que as pessoas não procurem abrigo embaixo de árvores, por causa do risco de queda e de descargas elétricas. Também é recomendado não estacionar veículos próximos a torres de transmissão e placas de propaganda.

Nas cidades sob alerta laranja, a recomendação é, se possível, desligar aparelhos elétricos e o quadro geral de energia.

Nas áreas sob alerta amarelo, a orientação é evitar o uso de aparelhos eletrônicos ligados à tomada.

Em situações de emergência, a população pode procurar a Defesa Civil pelo telefone 199 e o Corpo de Bombeiros pelo 193.

articles.title: 'He prayed before attack': Machchhar tells Netanyahu chilling flydubai cockpit ordeal
articles.summary: Flydubai pilot Captain Smit Machchhar spoke to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu where he described the incidents that unfolded inside the cockpit.
articles.body: Flydubai pilot Captain Smit Machchhar spoke to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu where he described the incidents that unfolded inside the cockpit. He also described how he managed to open the cockpit door despite suffering repeated blows to his head. Netanyahu praised his courage and said he had "saved so many souls".Machchhar told Netanyahu that the flight had initially been normal. The co-pilot then wanted to play a game that he said many locals play. While Machchhar was looking towards the front of the aircraft, he suddenly felt a heavy blow to the back of his head.Machchhar also told Netanyahu that the co-pilot had wanted to pray before the attack. He said he looked towards the front of the cockpit out of respect while the co-pilot prayed."...while he was praying, out of respect, I was just looking at the front and not at the back, and suddenly, after, I would say about four-five minutes, there was a big blow to the back of my head."My first thought was that there was a catastrophic damage to the aircraft and something is not right," Machchhar said.He said the blows continued and he soon realised that the aircraft had not been damaged. Instead, the co-pilot was attacking him."And that's when I realised that it's not the aircraft, it's the other guy who was in the cockpit with me," he said.Machchhar said the initial blows left his vision severely blurred, making it difficult for him to understand what was happening. He then felt the aircraft sharply descending."My memory is still in bits and pieces right now," he told Netanyahu.The pilot also recalled trying to open the cockpit door once, but said the co-pilot shut it again. He later found himself lying on the cockpit floor as he heard the aircraft moving rapidly and passengers screaming.Machchhar said he then realised he had to make one final attempt to reach the door."And as I was telling the ambassador here, that I had that one last fight left in me that, you know, call it personal or call it for people," he said. "But let's say I did it that if I don't do it, I'm going to die."He said he pushed himself towards the door and managed to open it. Crew members and others outside then took control of the situation."And thankfully people were waiting to bounce back, took over the control and the rest is what you know, sir," Machchhar said.'There is no pin'Netanyahu asked Machchhar how he had managed to open the cockpit door when the co-pilot was preventing access.Machchhar explained that the door has a twist mechanism on the inside and can normally be opened from outside only using a code. His colleagues outside the cockpit were trying to enter the code, but the attacker was preventing the door from being opened."The only way to open the door was to reach the knob and like any other knob, just to twist it open and it opens on its own," Machchhar said."There is no pin, but yes, the door, it was, it was a short, quick twist, but the point was to reach to that point, to reach to that place."Once he reached the knob, Machchhar said he was able to twist it open.Netanyahu invites Machchhar to IsraelNetanyahu repeatedly praised Machchhar during the conversation, calling him a hero of India, Israel and the world."I, frankly, I'm amazed at your courage, at your coolness of judgement under impossible conditions," Netanyahu said.He said Machchhar's actions had helped save lives and described the incident as an example of how courage could overcome violence."You're a hero of Israel. You're a hero of India. You're a hero of the entire world," Netanyahu said.The Israeli prime minister also said Machchhar would be welcomed in Israel and invited him and his family to visit.Netanyahu said he wanted Machchhar and PM Modi to light a celebratory flame at Israel's next Independence Day ceremony. articles.title: When parenting advice becomes too much
articles.summary: Many parents feel overwhelmed by the amount of parenting information available
articles.body:
Before Rosie Whitfield became a mum, she imagined herself parenting very calm children.

"Then I had two wild boys," she says with a laugh.

Following the birth of her kids, Rosie spent hours online looking for the best advice and was drawn to one particular approach to parenting: Gentle parenting, which focuses on empathy and mutual respect with little emphasis on punishment, albeit with boundaries.

But she constantly worried her choices, from sleep schedules to handling toddler tantrums, were "ruining their lives forever".

Rosie does not blame the gentle parenting philosophy itself but instead says the overall amount of parenting advice online was "overwhelming" and "made mundane parenting choices feel like the absolute end of the world."

"I felt like if I was choosing to put the TV on for 20 minutes while I did the dishes or had a coffee, I was choosing to destroy my children's brains," says Rosie, who is originally from Birmingham and now lives in Dubai.

Rosie believes her confidence and intuition were stripped away as she questioned every parenting decision. And she is not alone.

Government research suggests that around two-thirds of parents with young children feel overwhelmed by the amount of parenting information available and struggle with conflicting advice, with many turning to social media for support.

Research from the charity Action for Children found that many parents of teenagers who initially contacted the charity for help with school avoidance, ADHD or mental health, often went on to describe their own anxiety, exhaustion and uncertainty of how to parent with empathy and patience when close to burnout.

Faced with an array of parenting philosophies, or "brands" to choose from, is all of this advice helping parents or making them more anxious? And is there really a best way to parent? Or, as we strive to become the perfect parent, are we losing our intuition?

Parents today are confronted by parenting styles including "helicopter parenting", which is focused on closely monitoring and protecting children from harm, and "tiger parenting", which involves strict parenting and high expectations for achievement. There are also "snowplough parents", who try to remove obstacles from their child's path, and "dolphin parents", who aim to be firm but flexible.

Author Matilda Gosling, who wrote Evidence‑Based Parenting, says many of the parenting fads or trends complicate what should be a straightforward relationship between a parent and child.

"Some parents think 'I need to be a snowplough parent and plough all of these obstacles out of the way'."

"But it really complicates what is actually a fairly fundamental part of being human, which is that you are warm and you love your children and you put in place some boundaries around them."

Gosling believes parenting trends often represent a pendulum swing, with one generation trying to correct what it believes the previous one got wrong.

"Throughout history, you get these swings from one extreme to the other," she says.

Gentle parenting is seen by some as the latest swing away from a strict, detached parenting style popular in the 1990s, which often relied on controlled crying, the naughty step and time out.

It is built around understanding, empathy and respect but also emphasises the importance of boundaries.

One of the most widely studied models of parenting comes from developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind.

Baumrind identified three parenting styles, later expanded to four: authoritative (high warmth and high control), authoritarian (low warmth and high control), permissive (high warmth and low control), and neglectful (low warmth and low control).

"Authoritative is the gold standard," says Gosling who has looked at more than 1,000 studies.

Research has found that children raised with an authoritative approach, combining warmth with clear boundaries, tend to achieve better academic results, have higher self-esteem and stronger social skills.

But where gentle parenting fits within that framework is disputed. Gosling believes that it falls on the permissive side.

"It's very much child-led. The child ends up having so much control that there's no sense of safety coming from the outside."

However, Sarah Ockwell-Smith, who is widely credited with coining and popularising the term 'gentle parenting', strongly disagrees.

"It [gentle parenting] is not remotely permissive," she says, putting it firmly in Baumrind's authoritative category. Clear boundaries are "super important".

Social media, however, is flooded with memes of exhausted parents calmly negotiating with a child having a supermarket meltdown, something Ockwell-Smith finds deeply frustrating.

"I have to step away from the Instagram reels and the TikToks because I just want to comment, 'This is not gentle parenting'".

"You have house rules, family limits, discipline and consequences. But the difference is we look at discipline as learning and teaching rather than punishing."

Toddler tantrums and teenage behaviour, she argues, should be viewed through a lens of ongoing brain development, not 'they're being naughty' or 'they hate me'.

But despite the term being popular, Ockwell-Smith believes that gentle parenting is still a fringe movement and that authoritarian parenting remains the dominant style.

Around 80 years ago, American paediatrician Dr Benjamin Spock published a book called Baby and Child Care, which went on to sell millions of copies and became the main source of advice for mothers for generations.

The opening line was "Trust yourself. You know more than you think..."

The book challenged strict parenting norms of the time and in the following decades parents were offered more advice from an increasing range of voices.

Research into parenting has increasingly focused on the early years - from pregnancy to the age of two when the building blocks for lifelong emotional and physical health are laid down. For parents, that means more advice to navigate competing messages about what is best for their children.

Professor Ellie Lee, the director of the Centre for Parenting Culture Studies, has studied parenting for more than two decades, including research into mothers' confidence and uncertainty around infant feeding.

She says a major shift occurred in the 1990s when parenting became an increasing focus of public policy.

"Politicians started to say 'Parenting's the hardest job in the world. Children don't come with a manual. We need to give parents guidance. Parents need more support. We need parent education'."

Advice began to emerge on almost every aspect of family life, from tummy time, to feeding, to the right buggy, she explains.

Prof Lee argues that while some public health campaigns were necessary, such as advice not to put babies to sleep on their front after research into cot deaths, the growing culture of advice began to make parents paranoid.

"Dr Spock's 'trust yourself' philosophy is now a very counter-cultural piece of advice," she says. "What we say instead is 'always seek help',"

She believes this has made parents more anxious about doing things "right".

"Some of the things that are now presented as really high stakes are not," she says, using examples like breastfeeding exclusively for six months or how much tummy time a child needs.

"It's terrible because parents become completely exhausted."

Ockwell-Smith says the volume of advice can be "deafening and confusing".

"Actually, parents should just learn themselves and go on intuition," she says.

Others point out that there is also a problem of advice being given that is altogether wrong. Ruth Watts is a health visitor who began sharing content on social media after becoming concerned about misinformation online.

She had seen "experts" advise parents to wean babies onto solids early, offer treatment advice for tongue tie or allergies without medical training, and tell parents to put babies in their own rooms before six months.

Many families, she argues, are working longer hours while at the same time health services are being stripped back, leaving more parents looking online for breastfeeding, behaviour and sleep support.

"We are looking for that kind of personable, conversational approach from people, rather than reading a website."

Many factors shaping family life remain outside parents' control. A child's temperament, special educational needs, family support, finances and their own upbringing can all influence family life.

While some say parenting hasn't got harder but expectations have, others argue that parents today are facing more complex challenges than in previous generations with growing concerns around young people's mental health.

There are also debates around children spending more time on screens and less time outdoors, while schools are reporting increasing behavioural challenges and lower respect for rules and authority. Prof Lee believes parental confidence is at an all-time low.

"I think parents feel very nervous about disciplining children now because they're worried about how it's going to make them feel," she argues.

The confusion around the "right" way to parent has led some parents to turn to courses for help.

Aymara Lamche-Brennan, who has a 22-year-old daughter, four-year-old son and six-month-old daughter, signed up for a course during the summer when another mother at the school gate mentioned she was attending.

"The flyer said 'it's the toughest job in the world' and I thought yes it is, how can you help?'" Aymara says from her home in London.

"When I had my daughter, I was 19 and I didn't really think much about parenting styles, she was with me everywhere and I just kind of rolled with it, but what I really want to know now is what simple wins are there with parenting?"

Aymara said the Circle of Security course she attended gave her practical tools so she could help her children organise their feelings, take charge when she needs to and recognise when she was becoming stressed.

"It's not telling you how to parent. It's helping you think," says Jennifer Peters, a former social worker and director of the charity Connected Lives which runs courses across London, Derbyshire and Cambridgeshire.

She says most parents want the best for their kids but they don't always know how to get there, and that guidance can be helpful.

"I don't think people need to be bombarded with information but the group experience helps you think, 'oh, it's not just me' and lets you take a step back from it all," Peters says.

Back in Dubai, Rosie says the arrival of her second child changed everything as she realised her sons were "polar opposites" and there is no one-size-fits-all solution.

A recent trip home to Birmingham also provided some perspective. Her eldest son was throwing a tantrum, and Rosie found herself wrestling with a familiar worry.

"If I send him upstairs, am I damaging him emotionally? Is he going to develop an attachment disorder because of this?"

But her mum said, 'Just send him upstairs. He can't hit his brother over the head with a horse [if he is upstairs]. Follow through with your actions.'

Rosie is taking this "generational advice" on board and has started "venting on social media" to show other mums that they are not alone.

Looking back on her first few years of being a mum, she said she wished she had known one thing.

articles.title: The Celebrity Traitors connections that might surprise you, from Jerry Hall and Richard E Grant to Rob and Romesh
articles.summary: Lots of the stars have worked together, some are good friends - and that can impact the show's dynamics.
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first two episodes of The Celebrity Traitors

"I know Rob very, very well. I mean, I've sat next to him as he's had a colonic."

That was Romesh Ranganathan , reminding us - in case we were in any doubt - of his close friendship with Rob Beckett in the opening episode of The Celebrity Traitors.

His words sum up the key difference between this series and the regular civilian version. In Celebrity Traitors, the players aren't just on-screen competitors - many actually know each other outside the show.

Lots have worked together, and some are even friends. And those previous connections can have a huge impact on the show's dynamics.

It's also partly why it is quite so delightful to watch - as friendships unravel, and former co-stars turn on each other.

We've been unpicking the six degrees of separation. Here are some of the connections we've found - if you spot any more, we'd love to know. Get in touch with your thoughts in the comments section below.

The dynamic between Rob Beckett and Romesh Ranganathan is one of the most enjoyable to watch play out this year.

As well as being great friends in real life, they have also worked together repeatedly, including in their travel show, Rob & Romesh Vs.

They've also frequently made joint appearances on panel shows such as Mock the Week.

But their friendship could count for nothing in the castle, Ranganathan said ahead of the show.

"Rob is one of my best friends, and we've worked together for a decade now, but I still won't be able to trust it," he said.

"I mean, he's just as easily going to be on my side as he is going to twist the knife in my back given the opportunity."

Joe and James are also friends (for now)

Joe Lycett has said publicly that he's friends with James Acaster , and the pair have a running joke about how everyone gets them confused.

They’ve also worked together on the TV show Travel Man.

Lycett is also friends with Joanne McNally - he's described her as "one of my favourite people in the world".

But those loyalties could be about to be tested, especially now that Acaster has been recruited as a traitor (anyone remember how things panned out for "good friends" Alan Carr and Paloma Faith...?)

There are SO many comedians in this year's series.

And they are all likely to know each other. In addition to the alliances above, Joe Lycett was on the TV show Last One Laughing with Rob Beckett .

Joanne McNally and Romesh Ranganathan appeared on game show Unacceptable together, and James Acaster went on Ranganathan's hip hop podcast.

Speaking ahead of the show, McNally insisted she and her fellow comedians "haven't been in cahoots at all".

"We know that we're more than willing to throw each other under the bus," she said.

As for Acaster, he's admitted the other comedians are his “biggest threat” when it comes to being detected as a traitor.

“Romesh, Joe, Rob know me really well. They all know that I don’t change my mind overnight,” he said, as he pondered whether to turn and help fellow traitor Richard E Grant clear his name.

Maya has rubbed shoulders with several of the stars

It won’t surprise you that the two broadcasters of the group - Maya Jama and Amol Rajan - have met their fair share of the other stars before.

Rajan had previously hosted both Michael Sheen and Joe Lycett on the Radio 2 Breakfast show, and also interviewed Romesh Ranganathan on BBC Asian Network.

He's also been joined on the One Show on separate occasions by Ross Kemp , Miranda Hart and James Blunt - and earlier this year, he discussed AI on stage with Hannah Fry .

But in the end, Rajan became the first player to be murdered, before we really got to see the impact of those past connections.

Meanwhile, Maya Jama is best known for hosting Love Island, but she's also popped up in loads of other places - including at this year's Brit Awards, where she presented an award with James Blunt .

She's also been on Ranganathan's hip hop podcast, attended Milan Fashion Week with Leigh-Anne Pinnock , and she, Joe Lycett and James Acaster all appeared on The Big Fat Quiz of the Year.

But Jama played down her connections on Celebrity Traitors, saying ahead of the show: “I've met a few people in the cast, but nobody really knows me, so we're all starting from scratch.”

Usually the younger celebs in the castle tend to know fewer people, but Bella Ramsey is pretty well connected.

Notably, Ramsey and another younger cast member, Sebastian Croft , both starred in season six of Game of Thrones.

Ramsey also worked with James Blunt on the film Sunny Dancer, was interviewed by James Acaster on his Off Menu podcast - and had a funny chat about their "vegan-ish" diet with Romesh Ranganathan on The Jonathan Ross Show.

Ahead of the show, Croft said he didn't know many people aside from Ramsey before joining.

"One of the other things I'm excited about is this will be the first time I'm playing with people who, on the whole, don't know me and don't know how I work,” he said.

“I just don't believe Richard's a traitor. I've known him 30 years and he's my neighbour.”

That was American model Jerry Hall , speaking after actor Richard E Grant came under (admittedly self-inflicted) pressure in the opening episode of the series.

As well as being neighbours, the pair are linked in lots of other ways.

Grant was pictured leaving Hall's wedding to Rupert Murdoch in 2016; in 2003, they were pictured together at Chelsea Flower Show, and they also acted in children's film Tooth back in 2004.

"It was ridiculous,"Jerry said of the film. "We had such a laugh, and I went on holiday with him earlier this year, just after Christmas to Africa with some friends. And we danced all night. We had so much fun! Little did we know back then that we'd both be here [on Celebrity Traitors]."

Now they've taken the next step and moved in together, will they be arguing over who takes the bins out? We are here for it.

Romesh and Julie are connected by The Weakest Link

Yes, you know Romesh Ranganathan is the host of The Weakest Link.

But did you know actor Julie Hesmondhalgh is the voiceover narrator for the quiz show?

Here are a few other connections you may not have known about.

Hesmondhalgh and Michael Sheen both fronted Papyrus's online child safety campaign back in 2020.

YouTuber King Kenny was one of 10 online stars competing in the game show Would You Rather, hosted by Romesh Ranganathan .

And singers James Blunt and Leigh-Anne Pinnock are both Brit Award winners. Both being successful musicians, it wouldn't be surprising if they have mingled together at events over the years.

Where does this leave those with fewer friends?

While some of the celebrities have known each other for 30 years, others have no friends in the castle at all.

My Mad Fat Diary actor Sharon Rooney and Industry star Myha'la , for instance, have fewer connections than the others.

And that can be a disadvantage. Remember Niko Omilana and Ruth Codd last year?

After they were banished early on, a theory spread on social media that they were voted out because the other celebrities didn't know them that well.

Leigh-Anne Pinnock has said the fact she doesn't know many people might actually help her.

"I think I'm at a slight advantage because people just know me as Leigh-Anne from Little Mix, and they don't really know my personality that well," she said.

What's clear is that these prior connections are "exactly the sort of thing" that makes Celebrity Traitors so fascinating, as TV reporter Siobhan Synnot told me.

But - like Pinnock - she agrees that having loads of friends doesn't necessarily end up helping you.

"Quite often in The Traitors," she says, "that familiarity becomes a disadvantage".

articles.title: South Carolina football in free fall as Shane Beamer may be out of time with buyout decision looming
articles.summary: South Carolina football decision makers face mounting pressure after its eighth straight SEC loss, with Shane Beamer's $22.5 million buyout looming large.
articles.body: Another blown lead, another loss for South Carolina. What has ultimately turned into the story of Gamecocks football over the last two years once again caught up with head coach Shane Beamer on Saturday against Kentucky. Coming off a thrashing against Alabama last week, which came one week after losing to Mississippi State after holding a 16-0 lead, the dam seems to have officially broken in Columbia on different ways to lose a game. Leading 17-0 against Kentucky at home, South Carolina fans have grown accustomed to never taking a lead for granted. In this case for those wearing Garnett, it was as if the game was tied 0-0 given past instances of being let down by the results. BIG MONEY, BIGGER DISASTER: MINNESOTA EXPOSES MICHIGAN AS WOLVERINES ARE LATEST EXAMPLE OF WASTED NIL FUNDS And now, after Kentucky beat South Carolina 35-34 in overtime on a two-point conversion to move to 4-1, the chatter throughout the state will only grow louder for the Gamecocks’ athletic department to make a change at head coach. This was the Gamecocks eighth straight SEC loss, and also their 12th loss against Power-4 opponents in the past 14 games. If the Gamecocks were to fire Shane Beamer before the end of the year, he would be owed an estimated $22.5 million for his departure. To be fair to Shane Beamer, the program is not getting a return on investment with the money spent on players like LaNorris Sellers or Dylan Stewart, which reportedly hovers above $5 million combined. If anything, the football team has been robbed blind by Stewart, given his lack of production and antics on the field this season, and we just started the month of October. In hopes of putting an end to any distractions coming off last week's temper-tantrums along the sidelines in Tuscaloosa, Beamer suspended Dylan Stewart indefinitely this week from the program, with the head coach declaring he was the only one making a decision on when the defensive standout could return. But, it goes deeper than that. Those writing the checks are not going to sit with this, and pray for better days In this era of college athletics, a return on investment for those helping fund these player contracts essentially comes down to whether you make the playoff, or hoist a trophy at season's end. And no, I don't mean the Outback or Gator Bowl trophies. After a memorable 2024 season that saw the Gamecocks miss out on the college football playoff by just a few spots on the final weekend, the fans have witnessed a program going in the wrong direction. Finishing 4-8 in 2025, Shane Beamer declared that the national media, and those covering the program on a daily basis, would be changing their tune on the South Carolina program after they put together a 2026 season that would see them competing for both a conference and national title. "I can one billion percent promise you this... because of the success we're gonna have next season... we're gonna look back at this season and say, 'It sucked going through it, but because of what we went through in '25 it led us to what we just did in '26,'" Beamer said last year. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE And, even though we all understood what he was implying this past week, it obviously didn’t sit well with Gamecock fans when he discussed how good of a practice they had following the loss to Alabama. In reality, Beamer has always been confident that he was the right man to lead South Carolina back to the same statue as they acquired during the 2024 season. But, thanks to injuries, play-calling and some pretty bad luck, the 2026 campaign was crucial for his future. Different era means enhanced timing on decisions in college football Now, after the third loss in five games, those who control the payroll and fundraising at South Carolina will have a decision to make on what the future looks like for a program trying not to be forgotten within the SEC. Obviously, this is going to only create more chaos around the football building, especially when you are out of contention for a conference title before the second weekend of October. Schools know that they can no longer wait until seasons end to make these decisions, especially when you are trying to sell season tickets for 2027. At the same time, those within the program are already trying to detour players' agents from shopping them to other teams for next year, which has been the case according to multiple sources. And, it's not just at South Carolina. Discussions about player retention, the transfer portal, raises and movement are already taking place, and will only increase over the next two months. So, on the weekend of October 3rd, influential voices around the Gamecocks athletic department are already having to make a decision about 2027. Like it or not, that's the world we live in now. For Shane Beamer, his team will face Florida next, before they are due for a much-needed bye week. articles.title: 12-year-old girl killed in Baltimore shooting sparked by apparent parking dispute
articles.summary: A 12-year-old girl was killed and three others were injured when gunfire erupted amid an apparent dispute over parking at a Baltimore park Saturday, officials said.
articles.body: A 12-year-old girl was killed and three others were injured when gunfire erupted amid an apparent dispute over parking at a Baltimore park Saturday, officials said. Police Commissioner Richard Worley said two gunmen were being sought, and two different gun cartridges were found at the scene after the shooting near Leon Day Park. “What we know is that there was some type of argument between two cowards, and of course they both opened fire on each other,” the commissioner said at a Saturday night news conference. “In the crossfire, a 12-year-old little girl, who was probably down there watching football, was shot and killed.” Baltimore police said in a statement that a 25-year-old woman and two men, ages 23 and 28, were also struck. The woman was with the girl, Worley said. Worley said the adult victims had non-life-threatening injuries. The commissioner said, “The dispute most likely occurred from a stupid parking spot.” The mayor of Baltimore, Brandon M. Scott, expressed disgust at the situation and likened the gunmen to cowards, during the evening news conference. “Two men, or so-called men, got into a argument, and now this baby is gone,” he said. Coach Mark Brown of the Charm City Buccaneers youth football league said the gunfire broke out mid-game. “Some miscellaneous outsiders caused this situation,” he told NBC affiliate WBAL-TV at the scene. “It wasn’t us.” He said the youth league has operated for 29 years without something like this happening. “We strive to give back to the youth,” he said. He added, “This happened over a parking spot. It was avoidable.”

articles.title: France’s violent student protests raise warning for America: ‘A cautionary tale’
articles.summary: "The Big Weekend Show" co-host says the country's violent student protests are "a cautionary tale" for the U.S., warning open borders lead to unrest and misplaced anger.
articles.body: France’s violent student protests are fueling fresh warnings about the consequences of open-border immigration policies, with the unrest being held up as a "cautionary tale" for the U.S. "I would also say as we’re sitting here in beautiful New York City, this is a cautionary tale," "The Big Weekend Show" co-host Tomi Lahren said Saturday. She continued: "This is something we’re learning from Europe, and we would be wise to learn from Europe. They decided they wanted to have open borders. They decided they wanted diversity as their strength, and of course, Joe Biden tried that for four years. We’re undoing that currently." FRANCE'S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT Lahren posited that "when you let so many people come into your country, leech off of your system, then the people who are from there are going to at some point get upset." She said that anger often becomes misplaced and, "they end up lighting things on fire, which I think is stupid no matter what you’re angry with, but it’s no doubt these countries that say we’re going to be a global home for everybody, they end up paying the price, and it’s usually the native Frenchmen, or whenever they are that end up paying the highest price." Students in Paris began to protest late last month against what they deemed as overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, long school days and deteriorating conditions, blaming the government for not investing enough in education. REPUBLICAN GLEE ERUPTS AS WHITE HOUSE BOASTS SHARP DECLINE IN IMMIGRATION FROM MUSLIM-MAJORITY NATIONS The demonstrations started peacefully in Paris’ poorer suburbs but quickly spread to Paris itself, then went nationwide in cities like Marseille, Strasbourg, Tours, Nantes, Toulouse ​and Lille, becoming increasingly violent as they expanded. The protests were also fueled by the government’s 2027 budget unveiling on Thursday, which showed education spending would rise by only 1.7%, excluding teacher pensions, an increase which is below the rate of inflation, Reuters reported. Rioters have committed arson, vandalism, thrown objects at police and even assaulted people in some cases, prompting authorities to respond with tear gas and rubber bullets. TENS OF THOUSANDS FLOOD STREETS TO PROTEST SPAIN BORDER CRISIS More than 5,000 protesters were arrested this week across the country, according to Reuters, and more than 400 schools remained closed as of Friday. Euronews reported Friday that at least 65 school staff members, including 40 principals, have been injured since the unrest began, along with roughly 170 students. More than 100 high schools have suffered what Education Minister Édouard Geffray described as "severe damage." French intelligence agencies told a government crisis meeting Thursday that the protest movement had been initiated by politicians from the hard-left France Unbowed Party, known as LFI, Reuters reported Friday. LIZ PEEK: ANGRY, AFFLUENT AND ADRIFT — WHAT'S DRIVING SOME YOUNG AMERICANS TO VIOLENCE LFI has denied the allegations and accused President Emmanuel Macron's government of politicizing the protests ahead of France's 2027 presidential election. Simone Rodan-Benzaquen, senior envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that the unrest began with legitimate concerns but has since evolved into something far more serious. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The students’ grievances about missing teachers and deteriorating schools were real at first," Rodan-Benzaquen said. "But dousing a principal in gasoline and attacking firefighters are acts of extreme violence. What makes this politically significant is the effort to turn frustration over schools into a much broader confrontation with the government." Fox News' Efrat Lachter contributed to this report.

articles.title: Zimbabweans struggle to rebuild after fleeing xenophobia in South Africa
articles.summary: Returnees face economic hardship and limited support as they try to rebuild in Zimbabwe.
articles.body:
Mutare, Zimbabwe – Samantha Chimbuya had built a life in South Africa after leaving Zimbabwe in 2019 in search of better opportunities.

She found work, could afford food and believed her two children had access to better education. She also had access to healthcare.

As June 30 approached, a deadline set by anti-immigrant activists for undocumented migrants to leave South Africa, the 30-year-old packed her belongings and returned to Zimbabwe.

“It was not safe any more. They were raiding our homes, warning us to leave. It was scary,” Chimbuya told Al Jazeera.

Chimbuya was living in KwaZulu-Natal when anti-immigrant protests intensified. March and March, one of the groups behind the June 30 deadline, accused undocumented migrants of taking jobs and putting pressure on public services.

The deadline was not imposed by the South African government, which said June 30 would be a normal day and warned against intimidation and violence. But thousands of migrants left amid fears of unrest.

Some governments organised transport for citizens returning home. Chimbuya paid for her own journey to Hurungwe, in northern Zimbabwe.

By July 28, 116,670 Zimbabweans had returned from South Africa, according to Information Minister Zhemu Soda. Of those, 36,940 were assisted by the government, while 79,730 returned independently. A further 38,057 had registered for employment, Soda said.

For Chimbuya, coming home meant confronting many of the economic difficulties that had pushed her to leave in the first place.

She has struggled to find work and now relies on family and friends for help. Her husband remains in South Africa, where she says he is also struggling.

She had hoped to receive a grant to start a small business but said she had not received one.

Reverend Useni Sibanda, executive director of the Zimbabwe Christian Alliance, said many returnees had spent years abroad and were coming home without jobs or adequate support.

Some had not invested in homes or property in Zimbabwe while they were away, he said, leaving them with little to fall back on.

“They are coming back to a country where there are no jobs and where the social support systems may not be enough to accommodate them,” Sibanda said.

The government says it is trying to help.

Local government Minister Daniel Garwe said authorities were screening and profiling returnees to identify their skills and needs. Reintegration centres were being established, while the Ministry of Primary and Secondary Schools was considering recruiting qualified teachers among those who had returned.

Garwe also said companies were being encouraged to employ skilled returnees and that vocational training and support for people wanting to start businesses were being considered.

For some, however, the skills they acquired in South Africa have offered a more immediate route to earning a living.

Sidney Bunya, from Zvimba, northeast of Harare, left Zimbabwe in March 2020 because of economic hardship.

He moved first to Johannesburg, where he took various jobs, before settling in Port Elizabeth. There, a cousin introduced him to professional carpenters.

Bunya honed his skills and eventually secured large projects, specialising in roof trusses.

But in 2026, groups demanding permits began raiding his workplace. Bunya had only his passport, and employers became reluctant to hire him because of the harassment.

He bought carpentry tools, shipped them to Zimbabwe and left South Africa before the June 30 deadline.

Using his savings, he started a business at home. It now supports his family and employs five people.

“It was difficult to set up the business. But I am getting more jobs now,” Bunya said.

Motsi said churches had also partnered with local businesses to provide training in welding, carpentry and computer science.

Churches have been helping returnees with shelter, food and transport, but Ray Motsi, president of the Theological College of Zimbabwe, said the needs were overwhelming.

He criticised the government for not doing enough to support people returning after years abroad.

“We need a deliberate programme to reintegrate these people,” Motsi said, arguing that returnees needed more than transport home.

Rashweat Mukundu, a human rights activist in Harare, said the government should provide longer-term assistance, including small grants, agricultural inputs and machinery, to help people establish livelihoods.

The challenge, he said, was not simply getting Zimbabweans across the border but helping them remain economically secure once they arrived.

“I plan to open a grocery store, but funding is a challenge.”

articles.title: Houthis claim strike on Aramco site as Yemen fighting intensifies
articles.summary: Spokesman for Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen government says Houthi claims of targeting Riyadh are ‘misleading’.
articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthis have said they attacked an Aramco facility in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and Yemen’s Saudi-backed internationally recognised government intensifies.

In a statement posted on X on Saturday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had carried out a “military operation with ballistic missiles and drones” that targeted Aramco in Riyadh.

He claimed the strikes were “precise and direct” and “led to fires breaking out” at the site. A large plume of smoke and fire was seen rising near an Aramco facility in Riyadh on Saturday.

Later on Saturday, Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government, said in remarks carried by Saudi media that the Houthi claims of targeting Riyadh were “misleading”.

Early on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said its armed forces carried out 97 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi reinforcements on the Tor al-Baha front and the Taiz axis, using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers.

Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, the spokesman for Yemen’s government forces, said the attacks targeted “at least 260 Houthi fighters and destroyed or disabled 44 military vehicles”.

Late last month, the Houthis said they had attacked Aramco facilities in Yanbu, a Red Sea port on Saudi Arabia’s west coast.

Saudi Arabia said at the time it intercepted six ballistic missiles fired towards Taif and Yanbu and reported no damage to Aramco sites.

Earlier this week, the Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis attacked a power station in the Muslim holy city of Medina on Tuesday.

The fighting has intensified since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July.

In mid-September, the Houthis seized the port city of Mocha and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital route for global oil shipments, before anti-Houthi forces stabilised front lines.

Hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced since fighting restarted.

Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, forcing the Yemeni government to retreat to Aden.
