articles.title: Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio
articles.summary: US president tells a rally in Ohio that he believes there will be a ‘big surprise’ in the upcoming elections.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has continued rallying for Republican candidates while visiting Ohio, proposing a defiant outlook on his party’s chances in the November 3 midterm elections.

Trump told a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, that he believes there will be a “big surprise” in the upcoming elections, claiming his Democratic opponents do not know what is happening.

Polls have suggested that Democrats could gain ground in the midterms, but the US president said Republicans would do better than critics expect.

“Just get out and vote,” Trump said as he rallied for US Senator Jon Husted, gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and other Republicans.

“If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big,” he said.

Multiple incumbent Republican senators across the country face tough political headwinds, with Trump’s popularity falling in recent months as higher petrol prices and those for other staples persist amid the US-Israel war ⁠⁠on Iran.

Husted, a Republican in a competitive Ohio race against Democrat Sherrod Brown, hopes the president can motivate supporters who might otherwise skip midterm elections.

Trump garnered more than 55 percent of the Ohio vote in the 2024 presidential election, but economic concerns since then have sunk his approval ratings.

Ohio petrol prices increased 35 percent over the past year to $4.16 per gallon (3.8 litres) on average, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which compiles data ⁠⁠on automobile travel. Trump’s trade policy with Canada has also led to retaliatory Canadian tariffs that affect about $3bn worth of Ohio exports, based ⁠⁠on 2025 figures, Canadian broadcaster CBC reported.

Talking to reporters shortly before addressing Saturday’s rally, Husted said the US has to win the Iran war “on our terms” and, in the interim, he is “showing people that I’m fighting for lower prices”.

Trump extensively promoted his administration’s action on data centres, mainly those built for AI, during the rally, saying he was seeking to ensure they “benefit local communities” and praising Husted for an unsuccessful attempt to push forward legislation on the issue.

“Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” he said, repeating his defence of data centres.

Data centres have become a hot political issue, drawing bipartisan opposition in races across the country, with voters concerned about their impact on electricity prices, farmland and water supplies.

The issue became especially acute in Ohio, where Husted has been repeatedly attacked for his role in attracting data centres to the Midwestern state as lieutenant governor.

The Republican-controlled Senate tried to advance legislation this past week sponsored by Husted that would ask utility regulators to effectively charge large power users more, as consumers struggle with high energy costs. But it was blocked by nearly all Democrats.

“Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centres in Ohio,” Brown wrote on X on Friday, ahead of Trump’s visit. “Now, he’s making Ohioans foot the bill.”

images.caption: US President Donald Trump applauds as the crowd cheers during a rally at Butler High School in Vandalia, Ohio, US, on October 3, 2026 [Nathan Howard/Reuters]

articles.title: Epidermolysis bullosa: I was told my baby was as fragile as glass
articles.summary: Ciara says she found it hard to imagine her son being happy but has started to believe he could be.
articles.body:
When Ciara's son Ralph was born, he had skin missing from his hands and feet. Doctors said he was as fragile as glass.

Ralph was diagnosed with junctional epidermolysis bullosa (JEB), also known as butterfly skin, at a few days old.

Ciara and her partner Lewis had to become experts in the rare genetic disorder, which causes skin to tear or blister at the slightest touch.

"We were new parents, we had never heard about this before and we had basically been told my son was like glass," Ciara, from Arlesey in Bedfordshire, says.

The 30-year-old mum is now calling on the government to increase funding and research into rare skin conditions, with the hope of one day finding a cure.

Five minutes after Ralph was born, following what Ciara describes as a normal pregnancy, she noticed "big raw patches" on his hands and feet.

"My partner Lewis went to the NICU [neonatal intensive care unit] with him and left me with a picture of him," she says.

"I spent the whole time looking at that picture questioning what on earth was going on."

After being put in a heated incubator, Ralph's body broke out in head-to-toe blisters.

Two days later, the couple received a diagnosis of epidermolysis bullosa, with the specific subtype of junctional epidermolysis bullosa (JEB), of which there are two main forms.

Ralph's form is generally milder, rather than the severe type which can be life-threatening. But there is no cure and limited treatment options.

Ralph's parents grease bottle teats to avoid damaging his mouth and turn his baby-grows inside out to avoid friction from the seams. They spend up to three hours each night replacing bandages on his feet.

"At the start, when he was a newborn, everything felt so heavy. It was really hard to imagine him being happy.

"Doctors from Great Ormond Street were essentially saying 'we need to teach you how to care for him' and we were expected to learn it – the medical professionals around us at the local hospital were learning on the job with us," she says.

What is junctional epidermolysis bullosa?

Young people with the condition are sometimes called "butterfly children", due to their skin's fragility, like a butterfly's wing.

According to DEBRA UK, the charity for people living with the disorder, it leads to blistering across the body, alopecia, malformed fingers and toenails and irregular tooth enamel.

It is caused by a gene mutation which results in faulty or missing proteins in layers of the skin and internal organs. Ralph's DNA lacks the instructions for sticking his epidermis (the surface layer of our skin) to the dermis (the next one down).

Two of the most common symptoms are pain and itching from frequent and extensive blistering.

Ciara recently started a petition calling for more research into the condition and after reaching 10,000 signatures, she received a response from the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC).

The DHSC, which has also been contacted by the BBC for comment, said it had already committed £1.075m over five years for projects specifically related to EB.

It said research had so far covered advanced treatments, symptom management, supportive care and better care co-ordination.

But Ciara worries her son's rare condition could get "left behind" in the world of research.

"It feels like families like ours are the ones being left to connect the dots. It just doesn't feel good enough.

"If enough people knew how devastating this condition is, something would have to happen because no-one, no human in the world, would stand by and allow children to suffer from birth for the rest of their lives.

"If the system in place is working, why are families like ours still having to work so tirelessly to raise awareness, contact researchers and campaign for anything that might improve our children's quality of life?"

Tony Byrne, chief executive officer of DEBRA UK, says research is "not an abstract ambition" for people with butterfly skin, but "the route to less pain, better treatments, and the hope of a cure".

"This petition matters because dedicated, ring-fenced government investment would give researches greater certainty, help promising discoveries move into UK clinical trials and ensure rare conditions are not overlooked," he adds.

Despite how painful the condition is and the need for more research, Ciara says she has finally started to believe that Ralph can live a happy life.

"He is just the most stubborn, funny, resilient little boy. He loves simple things. When the trees move in the wind, it makes him so happy," she says.

"Ralph can have the most awful wounds on his stomach or his elbows and he's still rolling over trying to get toys. He doesn't let anything stand in his way. He's so fragile, but so desperate to move.

"Despite everything he's so happy, he's so smiley. He won't let anything hold him back."

articles.title: Cambridgeshire teenage artist finds confidence in illustrating
articles.summary: Bethany's work is published after her talent was spotted by an author visiting her school.
articles.body:
A 15-year-old girl who previously experienced situational mutism is now a published book illustrator after finding the confidence to share her artwork through storytelling.

Bethany, a student in Cambridgeshire, illustrated The Bestest Story in the World... Ever! written by Chip Colquhoun and published last month.

Colquhoun asked Bethany to illustrate his book after she drew a portrait of him while she was in the audience listening to him deliver a storytelling session at her school.

The teenager said seeing her illustrations in print was "really weird and surreal".

When speaking to BBC Radio Cambridgeshire's Louise Hulland, Bethany explained she drew Colquhoun as a way to concentrate on the session.

"Drawing at that point helped me focus, so I needed something to draw and he was right there," said Bethany.

She described her drawing of the Colquhoun as "very stylised", adding: "[It is] not really the style I draw in now, but it was. I would say it's pretty good for the skill set I had then."

Colquhoun said: "She wowed me first with the portrait of me that she created."

He added that he was "excited" by the idea that Bethany had used drawing to help her focus.

Bethany's portrait was used in one of the author's books, which detailed advice for educators on how to use storytelling as a teaching tool.

The 15-year-old explained she had been situationally mute when she was younger, adding: "I'd speak to certain people and then not really talk to others. It was mainly people I didn't feel comfortable with or didn't know that I didn't speak to."

She added: "I mean [illustrating] definitely improved my confidence a lot and I think it's just improved me as a person a little bit as well, because I'm able to do things I haven't done before.

"If I was here a few years ago, I wouldn't be doing this because I would be too nervous and I would be too stressed."

Bethany is now working on illustrations for a third book, as well as three drawings for another project.

She said she was managing to intersperse her drawing with her schoolwork.

"I mostly work later in the night, so 8-9ish for the drawings and then leave the schoolwork to the earlier points because I have more energy during later times," she said.

articles.title: California sanctuary is removing purple sea urchins to help restore kelp; 117,847 pounds have been added to compost
articles.summary: California sanctuary is removing purple sea urchins from areas targeted for kelp restoration and giving them a second use as compost.
articles.body: California sanctuary is removing purple sea urchins from areas targeted for kelp restoration and giving them a second use as compost. Since 2023, urchins collected from restoration sites in Greater Farallones National Marine Sanctuary have been transported to West Marin Compost in Marin County.Removing the urchins helps reduce their numbers near bull kelp, which gives the kelp a better chance to survive, reach adulthood, and release spores. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), a total of 117,847 pounds of purple urchins have been added to the compost mix as of July 2025. The animals also provide nitrogen, calcium, and micronutrients that enrich compost used by local farmers and gardeners.How are purple urchins being removed and turned into compostThe purple urchins are harvested by hand from areas selected for their high potential for kelp restoration. The effort is led by the Greater Farallones Association, along with Greater Farallones and Cordell Bank National Marine Sanctuaries. After being collected, the urchins are transported to West Marin Compost, where they are added to the compost mix. Since 2023, 117,847 pounds of urchins have been added to the compost. Reducing the number of purple urchins around bull kelp gives the plants more opportunity to survive, mature, and release spores that can produce the next generation. Commercial urchin diver Erik Owen has been collecting the animals for the restoration project since 2023. The harvested urchins are then taken to West Marin Compost, where they become part of the composting process.Why are purple urchins being removed from kelp restoration sitesPurple urchins feed on kelp, and their numbers can rise sharply when kelp forests decline because of different stressors. Greater Farallones National Marine Sanctuary has experienced a catastrophic loss of bull kelp since 2014 following a series of events. As the kelp declined, purple urchins became a dominant part of the nearshore environment and continued feeding on the remaining bull kelp. The restoration effort focuses on areas where kelp has a strong chance of recovery.Why are starving purple urchins composted instead of sold as seafoodPurple urchins collected during the restoration work have little commercial value because they are starving after losing much of their bull kelp food supply. They may remain in this condition for years and produce very little uni, a prized delicacy once obtained from healthy red urchins in the sanctuary and along the Sonoma and Mendocino coasts before the major kelp die-off.Local divers collect the urchins at restoration sites and send them for composting instead of exporting these animals for food. This gives the animals another purpose while supporting the restoration effort. Once composted, the urchins become part of material used to grow food, connecting kelp restoration with local agriculture.Purple urchins turn marine nutrients into compost for farmsAt West Marin Compost, the harvested urchins add nutrients to compost used by local agriculture. Jeff Creque, a consultant with West Marin Compost, said,"Urchins are a great source of nitrogen, calcium, and micronutrients. We are happy to have a bit of the sea added to our material". The composting effort gives the purple urchins collected from kelp restoration areas a new purpose by turning them into material that can support farmers and gardeners.The wider restoration project also involves work with Northern California’s Tribal community, research at sites where kelp has persisted, collaboration with commercial urchin divers to remove urchins from restoration areas, and kelp outplanting. Together, these activities support the broader effort to restore the ecosystem.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Lenny Rush helps get Eric Morecambe vampire book on TV
articles.summary: Gary Morecambe says writing the books gave his father "as much pleasure" as Morecambe and Wise.
articles.body:
The son of Eric Morecambe has revealed that actor Lenny Rush's involvement was crucial to finally bring his father's novel to the screen after 35 years of trying.

Gary Morecambe said he had been trying to adapt The Reluctant Vampire children's books for television since his late father asked him to in 1982.

The comedian, who lived in Harpenden when he wrote the stories, told his son they "gave him as much pleasure" as his celebrated work with Morecambe and Wise.

After several unsuccessful attempts to bring the books to screen, Morecambe said he had started to lose hope. But he said of the Essex actor's involvement: "Once we made him the star of it, everything then just fell into place."

The BBC series, adapted by Alan Partridge writers Neil and Rob Gibbons, stars Rush as Val, who struggles with his vampire identity only to discover he has been human all along.

The 17-year-old actor, from Burnham-on-Crouch in Essex, has had notable roles in Slow Horses, Doctor Who and the comedy Am I Being Unreasonable?

This year, he has filmed scenes as Dobby the house-elf for HBO's Harry Potter series at Leavesden in Hertfordshire.

Morecambe said: "Back in 1982 when my father wrote it, he did say to me, 'I'd really love to see this televised or as a film or something'.

"I think the key to it all really was giving it a completely different angle and that took the arrival and stardom of Lenny Rush."

Rush said he was told about the books by TV producer Shane Allen, who had been a fan in his childhood.

He said: "We had a Zoom meeting in late 2022 about maybe getting the rights to the book and making a TV series out of it, then in 2025, we were suddenly making it!

"And I'm so thrilled we've been able to."

articles.title: Gina Long  art exhibition at Bury St Edmunds cathedral
articles.summary: Ed Sheeran's paintings inspire Suffolk charity fundraiser Gina Long to create her own exhibition.
articles.body:
Gina Long has lived what she says has been a "very amazing life", but she never expected to wake up one day in her 60s and feel a desire to host her own art exhibition.

From raising millions for charity, being friends with football legend Sir Bobby Robson, to being appointed MBE, she has had a long varied career.

In 2020, it was global superstar and Suffolk's own Ed Sheeran who opened her eyes to the world of art and she began dabbling with paint from her Bury St Edmunds home.

The 64-year-old has since created more than 30 pieces of work ready for her debut exhibition, Square Peg Round Hole, being held for free at St Edmundsbury Cathedral on Wednesday and Thursday.

Six years ago, Sheeran donated one of his first abstract paintings to Long to auction for her charity work.

At the time, the painting, called Dab 2, was the only artwork Sheeran had made available for public sale, and it fetched £40,000 .

Inspired by Sheeran's abstract paintwork, Long transformed her greenhouse into a studio, and she said the rest was history.

"I woke up two and a half years ago and said to my husband Andrew 'I've got to paint Square Peg Round Hole', and that is truly how it has begun," she explained.

"It's all been so organically lovely, but a complete revelation in my life.

"I, in no way, thought in my latter years I would be an artist."

Long said this new chapter, and specifically this exhibition, had been about "painting the harsh, messy truth about life" and was for those who had felt out of place.

"I often say, I've lived a very amazing life, and I've failed at times, and I've succeeded," she continued.

"But I've rarely neatly fitted, and so on my canvas is the messy truth about real life."

The exhibition at the cathedral features 32 artworks, each with bold colours and interlocking squares and circles.

Helping set it up has been Emma Roodhouse, who was recently involved in curating the John Constable Hay Wain exhibition at Ipswich's Christchurch Mansion.

Long's main message is one of empowerment and she encouraged people to "put your head above the parapet".

"I hope it speaks to anyone also who's ever felt out of place, out of depth, and celebrating the act of simply showing up as yourself despite the pressures not to do so," she added.

Long was appointed Member of the Order of the British Empire in 2015 for charitable services, having raised more than £9m over the decades.

A close friend of Sir Bobby, who died in 2009 from cancer, she also created the Sir Bobby Auction in his memory to raise money for charities, including the Sir Bobby Robson Foundation.

articles.title: Rainbow sea slug find in Cornwall a reminder of climate change
articles.summary: Conservationists say the animal was discovered on a Cornish beach during an event.
articles.body:
The discovery of a rainbow sea slug at a beach in Cornwall is an "important reminder" of climate change's impact, conservationists have said.

The Rock Pool Project, a community marine conservation organisation, said the slug, also known as babakina anadoni, was found during an event it held at Porthpean Beach in August.

It said it was the first time a rainbow sea slug, which have previously been found in other parts of Cornwall and the South West , had been spotted at Porthpean.

Dr Ben Holt, chief executive officer at The Rock Pool Project, said while the discovery was exciting, it also showed how much the UK's shores were changing as climate change warms waters.

The Rock Pool Project said rainbow sea slugs were usually found in warm Atlantic waters off the coast of Spain, Portugal and France, but they have been appearing on UK shores in increasing numbers in recent years.

"Whilst this is an exciting find, it's also an important reminder of how much our shores are changing," said Holt.

"We must continue to track these changes to understand the effects of climate change on UK marine life."

Luke Galpin, who found the rainbow sea slug during the Rock Pool Project event, said it was a surprise to uncover it.

"I hadn't seen many sea slugs at all over the summer, so I wasn't expecting to find one," he said.

"But its unmistakable colour popped out at me the moment I flipped the rock over.

"It was tiny, about the size of my thumbnail, and in my excitement, I shouted for everyone else to come and have a look."

articles.title: The Kent village that helped shape Audrey Hepburn
articles.summary: Audrey Hepburn spent three years in Elham before the outbreak of World War Two.
articles.body:
Long before she became one of Hollywood's most celebrated stars, Audrey Hepburn was learning music and dance at a small village school in the Kent countryside.

The future Breakfast at Tiffany's and My Fair Lady actress spent part of her childhood in Elham, near Canterbury, where local historians say her love of performing was encouraged during three formative years before the outbreak of World War Two.

Today, a blue plaque on a cottage near the King's Arms pub marks the place where Hepburn lived between 1936 and 1939.

"It really was the starting point for the young Audrey Hepburn that she became," said Brian Badham, of Elham Historical Society.

Hepburn, then known as Audrey Ruston-Hepburn, arrived in the village after her parents separated.

Badham said it was decided she should continue her English education in Kent, where family friends were living.

She moved into Orchard Cottage with the Butcher family, among a number of Elham residents who offered accommodation to visitors before the war, according to local accounts.

She attended Rigden School in the centre of Elham where, Badham said, she would have had her lessons.

"One of the sisters encouraged Audrey to get involved with music and dance. That really was the starting point for the young Audrey Hepburn that she became," he said.

Fellow historian Dilys Webb said Elham offered plenty for a young girl growing up in the late 1930s.

"I think it was far busier than it is today," she said.

"There were more shops, coffee houses and pubs. In Audrey's day I think it was more contained and everything that was here that she needed.

"She had quite a nice social life. She did ballet, she obviously went to the coffee houses and socialised with her friends, so I think there was plenty here for her in the few years she was here."

The wartime years would take Hepburn far from Kent and shape the rest of her life.

As war approached her mother, a Dutch baroness, arranged for her to return to the Netherlands, then still a neutral country, in December 1939.

After Germany invaded in May 1940, Hepburn spent much of her teenage years under Nazi occupation.

She later helped the Dutch resistance by carrying messages and taking part in secret ballet performances to raise money for anti-Nazi causes.

The future actress also endured severe hardship during the war, suffering malnutrition as food shortages swept the occupied country.

Her son Luca Dotti once said in an interview: "She believed very much that there is a struggle between good and evil and you have to take sides."

Although historians are unaware of her ever returning to Elham, residents remain "incredibly proud" that one of the world's best-known actresses once called their community home.

Webb said: "Obviously when she was here the village didn't know she was going to be a superstar. Now everybody knows of Audrey and we are a very, very proud village."

Badham added: "She was very special. A wonderful lady and fondly loved by the people that she met while she was here.

"A short time but a lasting impact on their lives."

articles.title: Oxfordshire and Kenya villages' twinning anniversary library set to open
articles.summary: Kennington residents fundraise for the much-needed resource which will open on 10 October.
articles.body:
The first anniversary of the twinning between two villages is set to be marked with the opening of a new library and resource centre.

In October 2025, Kennington in Oxfordshire officially twinned with Musanda in western Kenya - the heart of Abingdon-based charity The Nasio Trust's community work.

In 2024, Oxford author Sylvia Vetta jointly lead a project with the charity to deliver Cosmic Cats - an anthology of stories by Kennington and Kenyan students, aiming to raise funds for the facility.

The author, who will cut its ribbon on 10 October, said the twinning committee chair, the Rev Sansom Kuponiyi, had come up with the twinning motto "bridging cultures, building friendships".

The trust writes that the connection between the two villages "is a story years in the making".

Vetta was the chair of the former Kennington Overseas Aid, which for 50 years raised money for development projects all over the world.

She said that when presented with a choice between three projects, people had voted for the Nasio one and built a production factory for the superfood spirulina in Musanda.

The charity founder, Nancy Mudenyo Hunt, who grew up in the Kenyan village, delivered the project and went onto to co-write a book with Vetta.

The Kennington community also continued the support and helped towards establishing the much-needed library, which will have WiFi access and a space for training sessions.

"Cosmic Cats is going to be the first book in the library because it's important that children know it belongs to them," Vetta said.

She said they hoped visitors to the Oxford Indie Book Fair on 22 November would pay for one book on a subject of their choice to go in the library.

Isaac Aldred, 19, from Kennington, spent a month in Musanda between February and March.

"From agriculture projects to jigger removal, spirulina making, and peer education, I saw firsthand the diverse range of Nasio's projects and wide-reaching impact," he said.

He said the "kindness and hospitality shown by everyone was inspiring".

"Despite the multitude of challenges facing the community, the resilience and determination people have is obvious."

He added he had seen the new project "that the people of Kennington have worked incredibly hard to fundraise for", as it had neared completion.

Vetta said "the most moving" example of the villages' friendship had happened on Remembrance Day, when at the war memorial the names of Kenyan soldiers from Musanda had been read out along with those from Kennington.

"This will be an evolving thing," she said, calling the children in Musanda "ambitious and all hard-working".

Hunt called the new resource "a tangible result" of their friendship.

"For 25 years, Nasio has believed in giving children access to education and opportunity.

"This library brings that belief to life and shows what can happen when two communities, thousands of miles apart, work together," she said.

The anniversary event will be celebrated at the Kennington Village Centre, via a video link with Musanda.

articles.title: The Feeling say Twelve Stops and Home was recorded in Horsham shed
articles.summary: The Feeling's debut album turns 20 as the band prepare for Eastbourne and Margate shows.
articles.body:
The Feeling's triple-platinum debut album was recorded in a shed in Horsham, according to frontman Dan Gillespie Sells.

Speaking to BBC Radio Sussex as the record marks its 20th anniversary, Gillespie Sells said it came from "a very different world" when music fans bought CDs and "nobody had an iPhone".

The singer said much of Twelve Stops and Home was made at the Sussex home of brothers and bandmates Kevin and Ciaran Jeremiah.

The Feeling will perform the album in full when a 20th anniversary tour visits Eastbourne and Margate in November.

Gillespie Sells, the only member of the band not originally from Sussex, said he spent many of his teenage years in the county after meeting his future bandmates at the Brit School.

He said the group began spending time together in Ashdown Forest before starting to record music in Sussex.

Asked whether he had visited the studio again since making the album, he said: "It wasn't a studio, it was a shed."

"It was an outhouse. There were brick walls but it was essentially a shed," he added.

Gillespie Sells said the recordings took place in the Horsham garden building owned by the Jeremiah brothers' parents.

"We borrowed some microphones, Kevin had built a small computer and we recorded the first album like that, basically just hanging out together," he said.

Released in June 2006, Twelve Stops and Home reached number two in the UK charts and eventually achieved triple-platinum status.

The album produced hits including Sewn, Fill My Little World, Never Be Lonely and I Love It When You Call.

Reflecting on its 20th anniversary, Gillespie Sells said: "It's extraordinary. I think about what a different world it was then. All those albums we sold were physical copies and nobody had an iPhone."

He said the industry had changed significantly since the album's release but its songs had continued to attract new listeners.

"I see people in their 20s who seem to know every word and I think 'you must have been a toddler when this came out, how on earth are you singing along?' but they do," he said.

The band's anniversary tour visits Eastbourne's Winter Garden on 11 November and Margate's Drill Hall on 12 November.

articles.title: Bees create a buzz at Liverpool St Johns Shopping Centre
articles.summary: Staff at St John's Shopping Centre in Liverpool staff are keeping busy with their rooftop tenants.
articles.body:
A Liverpool shopping centre's lesser known tenants are creating a buzz.

St Johns Shopping Centre has thousands of bees in hidden hives on the roof and some of the staff have even had beekeeper training.

Two hives were installed in 2021 and a third was set up last year. During summer peaks the hives become home to about 180,000 of the striped insects.

They produced a bumper amount of honey this year - enough for 150 jars of the sweet nectar - and local school children are helping design the labels.

The project was developed by St Johns and NG Bailey, who provide maintenance support to the site, after they wanted to do something for the environment.

Two hives were initially installed and staff were recruited to train as beekeepers. A third hive was added last year, with five members of staff now trained to look after them.

Kieron Jones, maintenance supervisor, told BBC Radio Merseyside : "I never thought it would be part of my maintenance routine to look after beehives.

"When it was suggested, it piqued our interest and we thought this is another skill set we can get, and it lets us give something back, so it was really good."

The hives are positioned on the roof of the shopping centre, in the shadow of the famous St Johns Beacon.

Sustainability manager, Suzanne Moses said it has been exciting for the team to learn new skills and it has brought them together.

She said the shopping centre's rooftop was "a great spot".

"[The bees] get the sunlight. When we tell shoppers and the public, they're always surprised by what's above them."

This year, the bees have produced 150 jars of honey – all of which is done in a workshop on the centre roof.

The jars will be given away to staff, shoppers, tenants and charities.

"It's been a really good yield this year," said Suzanne.

"Children from Whitefield Primary School in Everton will be designing this year's labels, so it's a great way to get them involved.

"And another of our beekeepers... goes into schools to run workshops, so it's great to get that education to the next generation."

Kieron added: "As we come to the winter months, the number of bees will reduce.

"Summer peaks about 60,000 bees per hive, so we have about 180,000 bees across the three hives.

"That will reduce down to about 10-15,000 bees over the winter.

"We'll go back in January to make sure they're OK but the bees will be asleep from the end of this month so it does get a bit easier – and we have a rest with the bees."

articles.title: Data centre and homes plan compete for Charlton Riverside site
articles.summary: A data centre plan in Greenwich is the latest flashpoint in a debate about London's digital future.
articles.body:
A growing debate is playing out across London: As demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and digital infrastructure grows, what should happen when data centres compete with housing and regeneration ambitions for the same land?

In south-east London, a site designated for housing has become the latest flashpoint in the debate about London's digital future .

The proposed 100,000 sq m (1 million sq ft) data development on industrial land at Charlton Riverside has been dubbed "concerning", with Greenwich Council opposing the idea before the centre's planning application has been submitted.

Supporters say data centres are critical infrastructure that power technology many people rely on.

But critics question whether they belong in areas earmarked for new homes and have raised concerns about their energy use, water consumption and environmental impacts.

Data centres are not new. Telehouse's Tower Hamlets site was built in 1989 under different ownership.

Managing director Mark Pestridge said demand was accelerating rapidly due to London's position as a global technology and finance hub.

"If you think about everything you do on a daily basis, whether you want to look at your bank account online, you want to look at your medical records or book a GP appointment, or stream a video, that will all run through a place like this," he said.

"I think London needs to be at the forefront of this moving forward, I think we have an exciting opportunity that we need to develop to make it quicker for us to stand up buildings like this.

"There's a huge opportunity for London."

And as artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly used, there is a rising demand for large-scale computing infrastructure.

Data centre developers are particularly attracted to London because of the capital's dense concentration of businesses, financial services and internet connections.

Operators often want facilities close to the customers using their services, such as the controversial data centre approved for Brick Lane in Tower Hamlets in July, which is intended to provide faster internet connections for financial traders in the nearby City of London.

In Charlton, Greenwich Council said the proposal for a data centre was at odds with its plans for the area.

Tom Creswell, the council's cabinet member for planning and development, said they had plans to build about 8,000 homes, improve public transport, and create 1,000 new jobs in the Charlton Riverside area.

"Our priorities as a council will always be focused on serving local people and bringing meaningful opportunities to the beautiful borough we call home," he said.

A spokesperson for the data centre project said regeneration in the area had seen "limited" progress and highlighted that data centres had been designated by government as Critical National Infrastructure.

They said their proposal would both "help unlock the delivery of new homes" through road infrastructure and green spaces, and support the growth of the industrial economy in the capital.

"Together, this would make nearby development more viable and transform a disorganised industrial estate into an area that is hospitable to both current and future residents," they said.

Data centres are regularly criticised for using a lot of electricity and water and lots of Charlton residents are opposed to the plans.

One resident told Politics London: "From what I've heard, it's going to be very noisy with all of the generators, it's on 24 hours a day," while another said: "They use too much energy and where does the energy come from?"

A woman said she would rather see homes built on the site.

"There's nowhere for people to live. A lot of places are overcrowded as it is. People have been waiting. I think we've got enough technology going around, I really don't think we need any more."

A spokesperson for the government said claims that British data centres were "draining the country's water" were false.

"In England, they account for just 0.2% of non-household water usage, and many newer data centres use advanced cooling systems that require very little fresh water," they said.

"This does not mean a blank cheque for Big Tech. Developers must use water responsibly, and new developments must be considered through the planning system."

Pestridge said Telehouse's data centre had a closed water system and the yearly water usage from the nation's data centres was "less than the water lost to leakage in a single day".

He added that Telehouse's electricity came from wind farms in the North Sea and they had equipment to dampen sound for neighbours.

"We haven't done a very good job of educating people about how much electricity and water we use," Pestridge said.

Water companies in England and Wales lose more than 3bn litres every day through leaking pipes - approximately a fifth of all the water put into supply .

A full year of data centre potable water use is approximately 1.88bn litres .

A Water UK spokesperson said they "desperately" wanted to supply the resource needed by data centres, but needed authorisation to invest ahead of demand.

"After having reservoir applications repeatedly blocked, we have finally been given approval to build 10, which will take years to complete," they said.

The data centre argument in Charlton is unlikely to be the last.

As the physical home for the computing power used by phones, computers and AI, the demand for these centres will grow.

Yet in a city facing affordable housing shortages and competition for land, each proposed development is also likely to face questions about what London's communities need most.

articles.title: In 2014, Shonda Rhimes bought a 1923 Hancock Park mansion for $8.8 million; after restoring and expanding it, she sold the 12,000-sq-ft estate for a record $21 million in 2022
articles.summary: There are houses that make a statement, and then there are houses that quietly become part of Los Angeles history.
articles.body: There are houses that make a statement, and then there are houses that quietly become part of Los Angeles history. In Hancock Park, one such residence has now added another chapter to its century-old story. Once owned by television producer Shonda Rhimes, the sprawling estate changed hands for $21 million, setting a new record for the Wilshire neighbourhood and marking a remarkable rise from the $8.8 million Rhimes paid for it in 2014, states the Los Angeles Times report.A landmark home gets a new lease of lifeThe LA Times report mentions that the estate began its life in 1923, designed by celebrated architect Elmer Grey, whose portfolio also includes the Beverly Hills Hotel and the Huntington Art Gallery. Set across more than an acre and combining two parcels on a prominent corner lot, the property had the scale and architectural pedigree of a grand Los Angeles residence.Rhimes purchased the mansion from actress Patricia Heaton, best known for Everybody Loves Raymond. Over the following seven years, she undertook an extensive restoration and redesign, turning the historic property into a home that balanced its original character with a more contemporary sense of space and light, 2022 online report states.Restoring the Italianate villaThe report also states that working with interior designer Michael Smith, Rhimes moved away from the home's later Santa Barbara mission-style appearance and brought back the Italianate villa aesthetic envisioned by Grey. The renovation was as much about revealing the architecture as it was about updating the interiors. A wood front door was replaced with glass, allowing more natural light into the entryway. The ceiling of the first-floor loggia was removed to create a dramatic two-storey gallery, while glass-blown skylights further opened up the interiors.Inside, marble floors, Venetian plaster, elaborate crown moulding and carefully restored architectural details give the nearly 12,000-square-foot residence a sense of old-world grandeur without making it feel frozen in time.A compound built for entertainingSpread across three floors, the mansion contains seven bedrooms and 10 bathrooms, alongside a formal dining room, two kitchens, a library, playroom and a movie theatre complete with a snack bar. A separate guesthouse adds another unusual feature: a private hair salon, adds the report.The grounds are equally expansive. Two yards, a swimming pool, cabana, paddle tennis court and a secluded hedged garden transform the property into something closer to a private compound than a traditional city home.A record-setting saleIf we go by the online report, the property was initially listed for $25 million before the asking price was reduced to $23 million. It eventually sold for $21 million, making it the most expensive residential transaction ever recorded in Hancock Park's Wilshire neighborhood. The record had previously been held by Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos, who paid $15.95 million in 2015 for the former home of Antonio Banderas and Melanie Griffith. Sarandos would later play a significant role in Rhimes' career, bringing her to Netflix in 2017 through a major development deal.For Rhimes, the sale adds another notable chapter to an already extensive Los Angeles real estate portfolio. The Shondaland founder, whose television empire includes Grey's Anatomy, Scandal, Bridgerton and How to Get Away With Murder, has owned several properties in Hancock Park and also maintains a Manhattan penthouse. The $21 million sale ultimately reflects more than a celebrity premium. It is a testament to what can happen when historic architecture, thoughtful restoration and a coveted Los Angeles address come together under one roof.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and FacebookReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Kerala chief minister V D Satheesan has strongly condemned CPM leader P Nandakumar’s alleged remarks describing Malappuram district as a “nest
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Kerala chief minister V D Satheesan has strongly condemned CPM leader P Nandakumar’s alleged remarks describing Malappuram district as a “nest of fundamentalists and communalists”.In a post on X, Satheesan said the remarks were particularly concerning as they were made in the presence of CPM leader and former Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan, without any objection from him. “Strongly condemn the communal slurs made by CPM leader P. articles.title: An Atlanta mansion built in 1924 for Thomas Jefferson’s great-great-grandson faced demolition; in 2013, its new owners cut the 8,000-sq-ft home in two and moved it about 2 miles to save it
articles.summary: Some historic homes are preserved by restoring their walls, replacing their old roofs, and repairing the damage.
articles.body: Some historic homes are preserved by restoring their walls, replacing their old roofs, and repairing the damage. But the Randolph-Lucas-Jones House in Atlanta required something else. It needed a police escort, utility crews to lift power lines out of its path, and a roof hinged down so each half could clear the route. Built in 1924, the 8,000-square-foot mansion was moved about 2 miles in 2013 after its new owners stepped in to save it from demolition, according to the Georgia Trust for Historic Preservation.Built for a Jefferson descendantThe Georgian Revival-style home was built in 1924 for Hollins Nicholas Randolph, an Atlanta attorney and businessman and the great-great-grandson of Thomas Jefferson. The house was designed by architect P. Thornton Mayre, who also helped build the Fox Theatre. The home’s design was based on the plan of Randolph’s ancestral home near Charlottesville, Virginia. The Randolphs lived there for about a decade before selling it to Margaret Lucas in 1935. Her husband, Arthur, operated several cinemas around the city, according to Rough Draft Atlanta. She stayed until her death in 1987. The house later became a fixture of fiction, too. A painting of it appeared on the cover of Anne Rivers Siddons’s 1988 bestselling novel Peachtree Road.The sale and troubleIn 1998, the Lucas family sold the property to the 2500 Peachtree Condo Association. During this time, the house was shifted forward on its lot, with plans to use it as a clubhouse and an event space. Maintenance bills quickly ended that idea, and the house fell into disrepair. By the autumn of 2012, the association held a city demolition permit and was offering the house free to anyone who could move it.Roger Smith and his husband, the late preservation advocate Christopher M. Jones, got the news while they were at a function at the Atlanta History Center. City Council member Mary Norwood pulled Jones into a corner for a private conversation. “Mary came up to us and pulled Christopher away into a corner for a private conversation. She told him the house was going to be demolished, and I think he decided that night we had to save it,” Smith told the outlet. Their firm, NewTown Partners, focused on distressed historic properties. Smith and Jones were chosen as project partners in January 2013. They closed on the empty lot at 78 Peachtree Circle in Ansley Park on May 30, which became the house’s new location. They also agreed to donate a preservation façade easement to the Georgia Trust for Historic Preservation, so the exterior could never be torn down. The project reportedly had a $1.5 million budget.Taking a mansion apart to keep it wholeTo save the mansion, it first had to be carefully dismantled. Preparations began in July, when the crew removed the brick façade and slate roof, significantly reducing the building’s weight. The bricks were carefully set aside to be cleaned and reinstalled after the move. Adjustments were to be made inside: the second-floor doors and baseboards were pulled and numbered so each could return to its original spot. The frame was split above the first floor, and each section topped out at 19 feet.The move began on November 8, 2013. A temporary road was built across a vacant lot opposite the Woodruff Arts Center, giving the trucks a direct run to the new address. The trip was 2.1 miles and took seven hours, according to the Georgia Trust. The house was slowly moved using hydraulic lifts, the trust said.Setting the house down was the easy part. The comprehensive rehabilitation began in 2014. Smith and Jones sold their own home and rented an apartment behind the lot to oversee the work. Smith has described money as a monthly puzzle of what could be paid for and finished. “There was this misnomer that we had all this money to do this project, when actually it was a shell game every month to see what we could pay for and complete. This wasn’t your usual renovation; it took care and planning and research to get it just right. Every step felt like pushing a ‘55 Buick uphill. But it was worth every cent,” Smith said. Jones died in January 2019, a few months shy of the main renovation being complete, and never lived in the house. It was renamed the Randolph-Lucas-Jones House in his honour.You use AI every day. articles.title: Saudi-led coalition dismisses ‘misleading’ Houthi claim of Riyadh attack
articles.summary: The Saudi-led coalition spokesman says the Yemeni armed group is ‘attempting to divert attention’ from its losses.
articles.body:
The Houthis’ claims that the Iran-allied armed group has targeted Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh are “misleading”, according to the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki’s remarks came on Saturday after the Houthis claimed ballistic missile and drone attacks on an Aramco oil facility near Riyadh.

The group said the assault caused large fires as fighting between the Houthis and government forces intensifies in Yemen.

In remarks carried by Saudi media Asharq Al-Awsat late on Saturday, al-Maliki claimed that the Houthis are “attempting to divert attention from the scale of the losses and the growing public anger against them”.

The development comes after the Yemeni forces “executed 257 precision targeting operations ” against Houthi sites, movements, and military capabilities on Saturday, according to the spokesman for Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces, Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili.

He added that initial estimates indicate that the operations killed at least 700 Houthi rebels.

Meanwhile, al-Maliki said the Houthis’ “ties to external agendas” have brought “chaos and devastation to Yemen”, adding that “what the Houthis are facing in Taiz … drive them to seek illusory victories”.

Early on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said its armed forces carried out 97 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi reinforcements on the Tor al-Baha front and the Taiz axis, using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers.

The fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces has intensified since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July, displacing hundreds of thousands of people since then.

In mid-September, the Houthis seized the port city of Mocha and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital route for global oil shipments, before anti-Houthi forces stabilised front lines.

Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, forcing the Yemeni government to retreat to Aden.

articles.title: ‘If you manufacture a dictator, we will bury it’: Uddhav, Raj launch joint protest against CEC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Shiv Sena (UBT) chief Uddhav Thackeray and Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray on Sunday led a joint protest march in Mumbai
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Shiv Sena (UBT) chief Uddhav Thackeray and Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray on Sunday led a joint protest march in Mumbai against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, with participants demanding the cancellation of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Maharashtra.Addressing the gathering after the march, Uddhav Thackeray accused the government of attempting to create a dictatorship under the slogan of “Make in India”.“I think you will also remember that when Modi ji first became Prime Minister, he gave the slogan, “Make in India.” Remember? We accept that. But if, under “Make in India,” you are also going to manufacture a dictator in our country, then we have gathered here today to bury that dictatorship and put an end to it. Everything else under Make in India is fine. But if, in the name of Make in India, you are going to create a dictatorship, then consider that we have buried your dictatorship...”Speaking ahead of the protest, Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Sanjay Raut said the demonstration was a collective response to what he alleged were attempts to undermine democratic institutions, electoral processes and the constitutional rights of citizens.“This protest is against the Hitler-rule prevailing in the country, hijacking elections, keeping the Election Commission and the Supreme Court in one's pocket, running a dictatorship, stealing votes, stealing elections, and poaching MPs and MLAs. This is a revolt against all that, much like the one in 1857,” he told reporters.Thackeray questioned the appointment process of Election Commissioners.“I have a question mark over the appointment of the Election Commissioners. The Election Commission should be appointed through an election. Earlier, there was a committee comprising the Chief Justice of India, the Prime Minister, and the Leader of the Opposition. They (the central government) removed the Chief Justice from this committee. In place of the Chief Justice, they appointed a minister chosen by the Prime Minister. That minister is Amit Shah. There are hearings after hearings in the courts, but there is no accountability.”Thackeray also questioned how Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar was appointed and alleged that powers related to citizenship rights were being exercised through the Election Commission.“The first question is: How was Gyanesh Kumar appointed? Does the Home Ministry have the power to cancel a person's citizenship rights? They are using that power through Gyanesh Kumar, and that is why we do not want Gyanesh Kumar. Earlier, it was 'India Against Corruption', and now it is 'India Against Vote Chors'... The BJP does not know how to run a government... The way you are running the government is not governance; it is revenge...”The march, dubbed the Virat Garjana Morcha (Grand Roar March), began at Metro Cinema and proceeded towards the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation headquarters in south Mumbai. State leaders of the Congress and the Sharad Pawar-led NCP (SP) also participated in the protest.The protesters demanded the removal or resignation of Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the SIR exercise.Party flags were not allowed during the march, with participants and supporters asked to carry only the national tricolour.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: No room to roam: The cost of a crowded planet for wild animals
articles.summary: Over the past fifty years, the average size of monitored wildlife populations around the world has fallen by 73 per cent, according to WWF's Living Planet
articles.body: Over the past fifty years, the average size of monitored wildlife populations around the world has fallen by 73 per cent, according to WWF's Living Planet Report 2024. The report names loss and degradation of habitat as the most commonly reported threat, driven mainly by how the world grows its food.This finding raises a plain question. When animals lose the land, water and forest they depend on, what happens to them?A shrinking home, not a vanishing oneHabitat rarely disappears all at once. It is cut into pieces by farms, roads, canals, railway lines, power lines and growing towns. Each piece may still have trees and water, but it supports fewer animals than the original whole did.The 73 per cent figure also needs careful reading. It describes the average change across thousands of monitored populations. It does not mean that three-quarters of the world's animals are gone, or that three-quarters of species have disappeared. What it does show is a steady thinning, and the report describes such declines as an early warning of greater risk to species and ecosystems. The pressure it describes is gradual and widespread rather than the result of a single event, which is partly why it is easy to overlook. The report also notes that some populations have held steady or recovered where conservation has worked.“This is not just about wildlife, it’s about the essential ecosystems that sustain human life,” said Daudi Sumba, chief conservation officer at WWF.What changes for an animal that loses spaceThe effects usually arrive in a recognisable order. Food and water become harder to find, so animals travel farther to reach them. Their routes cross fields, highways and railway tracks. Animals with large ranges, such as elephants and big cats, are affected first, because they need the most room.Smaller populations face a slower problem. When forest patches are cut off from one another, animals cannot move between them to find mates. Over time a small, isolated group becomes more vulnerable to disease and to sudden shocks such as drought or fire. Wherever forest meets farmland or settlement, animals and people also meet more often, and not always safely.Elephants outside the fenceIndia's elephants show how this plays out. The country holds about 60 per cent of the world's Asian elephants, according to the last census in 2017. Most of them do not live inside protected areas. Government and press figures put the share outside reserves at about 80 per cent. That share matters for everything that follows. A herd that lives mostly outside reserves has no boundary between it and the land that people farm, travel across and build on.For these herds, a journey between feeding grounds can pass through paddy fields, village lanes, rail lines and overhead power cables. Official data tabled in Parliament in 2024 shows what that means. Over five years, the leading cause of unnatural elephant deaths was electrocution, ahead of train accidents, poaching and poisoning. Odisha, Assam, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu reported the largest numbers of electrocution deaths.The government has taken some steps in response. It has identified and ground-validated about 150 elephant corridors, the routes herds use to move between forests. The Railways and Environment ministries have also formed a standing committee to reduce deaths on tracks.Tigers on islands of forestTigers tell a more hopeful story, with a warning attached. The 2022 estimate counted at least 3,682 tigers in India, a record, spread across 53 tiger reserves. These reserves are among the best protected forests in the country.But the same assessment shows the limits of protection. Roughly a third of the reserves need stronger protection, habitat restoration or more prey for the tigers to feed on. A few reserves in Mizoram, Nagaland and Jharkhand reported almost no tigers at all. Summaries of the report also describe many reserves as small islands of forest, joined to one another by a limited number of corridors. A reserve with a healthy tiger population can send young animals out in search of territory of their own, and many of them end up in unprotected land among farms and villages.The record count and the weak reserves belong in the same account. Protection works where it is applied well, and the gaps appear where it is not.Where Kaziranga endsKaziranga's protection does not stop at the park boundary, and a new proposal from the Assam government has put that line under debate. The state wants to replace the default 10-km eco-sensitive zone (ESZ) around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve with a site-specific zone of one to three kilometres. An ESZ is a regulatory buffer, declared by the environment ministry on a state's proposal. It is not an outright ban: depending on the notification, activities in it may be prohibited, regulated or permitted, and mining is among those most strictly restricted.Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma says the 10-km limit applies only because Kaziranga has not yet been finally notified. He argues it brings populated areas such as Kaliabor, Doboka and Jakhalabandha under restrictions, and holds up civic projects like a proposed stadium in Bokakhat. The state says the park's boundary and its UNESCO World Heritage status will not change, and that the 10-km zone stays in force until a new one is notified. Some residents agree. Hundreds rallied in support of the proposal on August 18, saying the current limits get in the way of building homes and basic infrastructure.The opposition and conservationists are not convinced. Congress state president Gaurav Gogoi led a protest at the Kohora range and alleged that the change could give legal cover to mining. The state government rejects the charge. Conservationists such as Jadav Payeng and Kavita Ashok point to the annual floods, when rhinos, deer and elephants move to higher ground outside the park. A smaller zone, they warn, could cut off those routes.A 2025 conservation assessment notes that a smaller zone is not necessarily a weaker one if it is designed to protect the most sensitive areas. Whether it does will depend on the final notification, which will decide whether wildlife corridors, flood escape routes and wetlands fall inside the line.Wetlands and the quieter lossesSpace does not only mean forest. Globally, freshwater species have seen the steepest declines in the WWF report, and wetlands are often among the first places to be drained or built over.The report points to Chennai, where rapid urban growth has led to a large loss of wetland area. Wetlands shelter birds, fish and amphibians, and they also soak up floodwater for the city around them. When they go, wildlife loses a home and people lose a buffer.The cost to peopleWhen space runs out, people pay too. Government data tabled in Parliament showed that elephants killed 2,853 people in India over five years, with the highest toll in 2023. Many of these deaths happened in places where farms, villages and elephant routes overlap. The elephant deaths and the human deaths come from the same stretches of land, where both now depend on the same ground.The Environment Ministry has issued guidelines on managing human-elephant conflict, and it says compensation is provided for losses. These measures respond to the damage after it happens. They do not by themselves restore the space that animals have lost.Where space is being rebuiltSome efforts aim at the cause. West Bengal has begun a community programme called Gajamitra, or Friends of Elephants, in which local people take part in reducing conflict. Conservation scientists have also suggested low-cost methods for farmers, such as planting chillies, ginger or citrus around fields, which elephants tend to avoid, or placing beehives along field edges.The WWF report also records progress in India, where it says some wildlife populations have stabilised or recovered. It credits government initiatives, careful habitat management, scientific monitoring and community involvement. At the global level, the report calls for more effective conservation along with changes in food, energy and finance systems.What the evidence points toThe picture from India and from the world is consistent. Animals do not simply move on when their habitat shrinks. Their numbers thin out, they wander into danger, they come into conflict with people, or they disappear from places they once held. Where land is protected, connected and shared with the people who live beside it, some populations hold their ground or recover.India's own examples point in both directions: electrocutions and train deaths on one side, a record tiger count and recovering populations on the other. The difference lies largely in whether land is protected and linked together, and whether the people who live beside wildlife are part of the plan.The question on World Wildlife Day is how much room is left for wildlife, and who decides what happens to it.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Latvian PM on track to lead pro-Ukraine coalition after election win
articles.summary: RIGA — Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs was set to retain power and form a pro-Ukrainian coalition after his centrist United List secured the biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence in 1991.
articles.body: RIGA — Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs was set to retain power and form a pro-Ukrainian coalition after his centrist United List secured the biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence in 1991. With 97% of ballots counted ⁠after Saturday’s election in the NATO and European Union country bordering Russia, United List was on 35.3%, enough for 42 seats in the 100-seat parliament. A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray Ukrainian military drones flew undetected into Latvia. Latvia’s economy has ⁠underperformed its Baltic neighbours for more than a decade and ​Kulbergs ⁠has vowed to improve governance, cut red tape and reduce public spending, political scientist Roberts Kits said. “Kulbergs played on being a get-things-done type of guy and has persuaded the voters that ⁠he can do things differently, bring some fresh energy,” he said. “This means the responsibility is huge. ​People expect ⁠him to deliver, but the question remains ‌whether he has the team to do it.” United List appeared able to secure a parliamentary majority with either the nationalist National Alliance or the liberal Progressives, Kits said. Hard line on Russia Kulbergs ‌pledged continuing support to Ukraine and to keep a hard line ‌towards Moscow. “Any economic ties with Russia makes us weak. Yes, it can bring some extra money, but it’s a weakness Russia might exploit,” he told reporters at his party’s headquarters on election night as supporters celebrated the scale of the win. “It’s remarkably good. ⁠I was not expecting such a result,” Kulbergs said. Voter turnout was 51.8%, down from 59.4% in 2022. United List was followed by the populist, MAGA-style Latvia First, which was on 13.1%. Latvia First had courted the country’s substantial ethnic Russian minority in the run-up to the vote. Third in the ranking was the pro-Russian Sovereign Power party, on 11.7%, followed by the National Alliance, which promotes a hardline approach to the Kremlin, at 8.9%. Throughout his campaign, Kulbergs promised more anti-drone capability for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5% ‌of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels in NATO. His pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia ​should stop any aid to Ukraine and instead focus on tackling cost-of-living issues, particularly among the ‌country’s Russian-speaking minority. Although pro-Russian parties increased their ⁠representation, Kits said they remained sidelined and were unlikely to influence government policy. Latvia’s ethnic Russian minority ⁠is split between those who oppose Moscow’s war in Ukraine and others who voice frustration with policies at home aimed at limiting ‌their influence on public life, which ​many of them see as discriminatory. Latvia, with a population ‌of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea ​and Russia and Belarus to the east, with EU and NATO allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south.

articles.title: How photographer Tim Smith captured Bradford's daytime dance revolution
articles.summary: Tim Smith's shots of the early 'daytimers' bhangra scene in Bradford feature in a Tate exhibition.
articles.body:
For decades, photographer Tim Smith's images of Bradford's British Asian "daytimers" dance scene remained largely unseen. Now, some of those shots are taking their place in a major Tate exhibition examining the creativity and rebellion that transformed 1990s Britain.

On a bright afternoon in Bradford, shoppers moved through the city centre carrying bags, going about their day.

Behind a nearby doorway, another side of Bradford was pulsing to a very different rhythm.

Tim Smith remembers stepping out of a small nightclub beneath the Alhambra theatre after spending hours photographing a "daytimers" disco.

"I walked out into this bright sunshine and there's all these people walking about with their shopping bags, completely oblivious to what was going on just the other side of this somewhat anonymous-looking doorway," he recalls.

More than three decades later, images Smith took inside that hidden world are making another unlikely journey, from Bradford's underground daytimers scene to the Tate Britain art gallery.

His photographs feature in new showcase The 90s: Art and Fashion, which opens on Thursday.

Curated by former Vogue editor-in-chief Edward Enninful, it brings together more than 100 works by nearly 70 artists, photographers and designers to examine a decade of creativity and rebellion.

For Smith, who lived in Bradford for more than 40 years, the inclusion of his photos is also recognition that some of the cultural shifts reshaping 1990s Britain were happening far beyond London.

"I'm pleased because I think there's a big shout-out for Bradford," he says.

"These culturally significant moments of that time weren't just happening in London and Manchester, like many media people like to think they were."

Smith arrived in Bradford in the mid-1980s after studying photography in Newport.

A nomadic childhood and life among migrant communities in Newport's Docklands had drawn him towards documenting lives beyond the mainstream.

Through the then-recently established Bradford Heritage Recording Unit, he began photographing the city's South Asian communities at work, at religious gatherings, at weddings and in their social lives.

"I was quite appalled at the lack of any kind of documentation of Bradford's Asian communities beyond the stuff that you'd see in the local papers," he says.

The daytimers bhangra gigs came later, after a friend told him about afternoon club events for young British Asians.

Smith's first response was simple: "What's a daytimer?"

Cheap to hire while nightclubs stood empty during the day, the venues became spaces where a generation could gather and celebrate, but also shape a unique new subculture: dancing to music drawing on Punjabi and South Asian traditions but fused with contemporary British sounds.

What Smith saw was not simply young people celebrating being Asian, but proudly "being British Asian".

Among those he photographed was Rani Kaur, known as DJ Radical Sister, one of the pioneering women of the scene.

In one of Smith's best-known images, which will feature in the Tate Britain exhibition, she stands at the DJ decks, surrounded by young clubbers.

Another frame, shot from above in the darkness with flash, caught a room full of faces in a moment Smith could not inspect until the film was developed.

"Part of it's luck, but you earn your luck," he says.

"Every single face that you can see in it… just looks like he's having the best time of his life."

To Smith, the expressions seem to say: "We're here, this is us, we're having a wonderful time."

Yet he appreciates there is another side to the photographs, and to the rebellion they record.

Many of the young people attending daytimers gigs were moving between the expectations of family and community and the desires of a younger generation testing out music, fashion, friendship and independence on its own terms.

Smith understood that publishing a photograph could expose somebody who had never intended their presence at a club to become public.

"I didn't know everybody in the picture," he says. "I thought, 'I don't want to get them into trouble.'"

So, apart from images of people he knew were comfortable being identified, much of the work stayed largely out of public view.

Only decades later did those photographs acquire another life.

When some were exhibited at Bradford's National Science and Media Museum, there were, Smith recalls, "one or two grumblings".

But among those who had lived through the scene there was also a growing sense that this was their history to claim.

"Come on, it was our moment," was the response relayed back to him. "This is where who we are now began."

Time has now transformed the pictures from informal snapshots of an underground scene into historical documents.

And Smith believes the daytimers helped lay the foundations for the vibrant British Asian culture scene that followed.

He was, by his own admission, entering worlds that were not his, a young white photographer trusted with access to communities and spaces whose stories were rarely documented.

"I felt quite privileged being a photographer generally because it gives you access to worlds that aren't necessarily part of your world," he says.

Now those darkened daytime Bradford rooms will take their place alongside other defining names and moments in cultural history inside Tate Britain, home to the biggest collection of British art in the world.

For Smith, there is real satisfaction in that journey: from an anonymous doorway in Bradford to one of the country's great national galleries.

It is also a recognition that while much of the cultural establishment looked elsewhere, Bradford was slowly writing a cultural history of its own, and continues to do so.

articles.title: Welsh Tory leader Darren Millar criticises FM for independence push
articles.summary: Darren Millar says Rhun ap Iorwerth has failed to improve public services or help Welsh businesses.
articles.body:
The Welsh Conservative leader Darren Millar will tell the first minister to "get on with the day job" instead of focusing on the prospect of independence at a speech on Sunday.

Darren Millar is expected to tell the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham that "Britain needs Badenoch" and reaffirm his party's support for the UK.

It comes after First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth called for a "new deal" for Wales from the UK government at a Plaid Cymru conference, and said at a rally there was "no turning back" on the independence journey.

Millar will say in his speech that his party is committed to keeping the UK together and that Britain's legacy should be used to inspire future generations.

Millar returned to the expanded 96-member Welsh Parliament after May's Senedd election with a group of seven members - down nine on the previous parliament.

Polls at various points during the election campaign had suggested the party could face a wipe-out, in part because of the rise in popularity of Reform in Wales.

In a copy of Millar's speech seen by BBC Wales, he says the Welsh government must focus on fixing public services and defend the relationship between the four countries of the UK - saying his party "will never allow" the break up of the union.

"A plan to draw a slate curtain between Wales and the rest of the UK will cause more harm than good for our children and future generations," he says.

He points to rising NHS waiting lists, claims Welsh businesses have "continued to struggle" since Plaid came to power, and that ap Iorwerth had instead decided to "cosy up to the SNP and Sinn Fein" referencing the recent meeting in Cardiff between the three countries leaders.

"He then signed a pact to promote the break-up of our United Kingdom," he says.

"The whole jamboree was seized upon by Vladimir Putin's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, who gleefully spoke up on Russian TV about the prospect of independence referendums across the UK.

"So my message to Rhun ap Iorweth today is this - get on with the day job."

Referencing ap Iorwerth, Millar says: "He told voters in May that the Senedd election was not about independence.

"Well, either he didn't get his own memo or he deliberately chose to deceive people.

"Because just like the Pied Piper of Hamelin, the Plaid Piper of Anglesey has tried to hoodwink people."

Miller describes the UK as "more than a political arrangement", saying each helped to develop industries, abolish the slave trade, liberate Europe, and shape the modern world.

"We are a shared family of nations. For centuries, the people of Wales, England, Scotland and Northern Ireland have lived together, worked together, and traded together.

"Of course, there are those on the left who say we should apologise or be embarrassed about our history.

"But I say that it is a legacy and a heritage that we should be proud of and use to inspire the next generation."
